No finite-element solution enters the pipeline: Monte Carlo fields, importance samples and operator training data come from the PINN, and Abaqus serves only to verify the result. Monte Carlo simulation, the first-order reliability method, importance sampling and the operator give consistent failure probabilities down to $10^{-3}$ for the slope studied, but a 3% scatter in the factor of safety inflates a probability of $10^{-3}$ by up to a factor of two, and the absolute values refer to one mesh. A heterogeneous Bishop analysis gives failure probabilities 2.6 and 8.3 times lower although its critical circles follow the PINN mechanism, because a small difference in the factor of safety is amplified in the tail. The operator also yields the failure mechanism and displacement response conditional on failure.

offered.title: Operator-informed initialization for Fourier features physics-informed neural networks
offered.abstract: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) typically exhibit spectral bias, where some frequencies of the target function converge more slowly than others. In this work, we analyze the training dynamics of Fourier Feature PINNs in the Neural Tangent Kernel regime to address this limitation. We derive an explicit evolution equation to estimate the residual error in the frequency domain, demonstrating that the convergence rate of specific frequencies is primarily governed by the product of the differential operator's symbol and the spectral density of the initialization weights. Leveraging this theoretical insight, we propose an informative initialization strategy that tailors the initial weight distribution to the specific PDE being solved. With this method, we can diminish the operator-induced spectral bias, balancing the convergence rates across the frequency spectrum and achieving better prediction accuracy. Numerical experiments on linear and nonlinear partial differential equations confirm that this initialization strategy improves learning dynamics and approximation accuracy across frequencies compared to standard initialization methods, with no additional training cost.

offered.title: SAGE-PINN: A Singularity-free Axisymmetric Geometry-Encoded Physics-Informed Neural Network for Axisymmetric Multiphysics Flow in Cylindrical Coordinates
offered.abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) provide a mesh-free framework for multiphysics modeling, yet fluid flow in axisymmetric cylindrical coordinates remains largely unexplored because the governing operators are singular at the axis and momentum and energy are strongly coupled through advection and buoyancy. We introduce SAGE-PINN, a Singularity-free Axisymmetric Geometry-Encoded Physics-Informed Neural Network for this class of problems. SAGE-PINN removes the coordinate singularity by construction: the parity-preserving variable $s=r^2$ and a modified stream-function representation eliminate explicit $1/r$ terms from the trained residuals and satisfy mass conservation identically. Boundary-fitted analytical ansätze enforce the boundary conditions exactly, while staged momentum-thermal-joint training, residual normalization, Péclet- and Richardson-number continuation, and a physics-scaled drift guard stabilize the coupled optimization. The framework is trained without labelled data, using only physics and boundary constraints, and its predictions are validated against finite-element reference solutions for steady nanofluid flow and heat transfer through a stenosed artery over a wide range of flow and thermal regimes, without case-specific tuning. Mass conservation remains at single-precision round-off, and over the central operating range the axial velocity and temperature are reproduced within $1.6\%$ and $9.1\%$ relative $L_2$ error, respectively. The main deterioration occurs only in the limiting regimes of strongly buoyancy-influenced slow flow and highly advection-dominated heat transfer. Embedding cylindrical geometry, conservation structure, and boundary physics directly into the network provides a robust route to PINN simulation of axisymmetric multiphysics flows.

offered.title: Error Estimates in Physics-Informed Neural Networks to Heat-Wave Fluid-Structure Interactive System
offered.abstract: We study a physics-informed neural network (PINN) approximation of a coupled PDE system that models the interaction between fluid and elastic dynamics. The canonical heat-wave model considered here couples a parabolic and a hyperbolic equation through transmission conditions on a fixed boundary interface, and serves as a prototype for the Stokes-elastic systems that arises in real world applications. This coupling makes the error analysis more delicate than that for a single PDE. We bound the error between the exact and PINN solutions by the associated PINN residuals, and we moreover prove that the generalization error is controlled by the training error, the number of quadrature points, and the size of the network. {To the best of our knowledge}, these are the first error estimates for a PINN approximation of a coupled fluid-structure interaction PDE system. We also show that numerical experiments with respect to a given test problem.

offered.title: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Free-Boundary Partial Differential Equations
offered.abstract: We study free-boundary problems within a physics-informed framework using Kolmogorov-Arnold network (KAN) approximations. The proposed approach incorporates obstacle constraints, partial differential equation (PDE) inequalities, complementarity conditions, and boundary conditions through residual-based loss functions. We consider a linear elliptic obstacle problem, a nonlinear $p$-Laplacian obstacle problem, and a time-dependent one-phase Stefan problem. The proposed KAN solver is compared with physics-informed neural network (PINN) and residual-network baselines. Numerical experiments show that KANs achieve low relative $L^2$ and $L^\infty$ errors while accurately resolving contact regions and moving interfaces. The results indicate that KAN representations provide an effective alternative for solving free-boundary PDEs.

offered.title: Component-Level Evaluation of Adaptive PINN Training for CFD-Oriented Crystal Growth Simulation
offered.abstract: Physics-informed neural network (PINN) training minimizes a weighted combination of partial differential equation (PDE), boundary-condition, and initial-condition losses. Because adaptive methods modify these weights during training, their weighted total losses are not always directly comparable. We compare fixed-weight PINN, gradient-normalized PINN (GNPINN), and a rule-based adaptive controller (AgenticPINN) under matched settings on a heat-equation benchmark and a simplified Czochralski-oriented thermal-fluid problem. In the crystal-growth MLP experiment, adaptive control reduced the PDE residual from the order of $10^{-5}$ to $10^{-6}$, while the boundary-condition loss increased from the order of $10^{-5}$ to $10^{-2}$. On the heat-equation benchmark, GNPINN achieved the lowest relative $L_2$ field error (0.054), whereas AgenticPINN obtained the smallest PDE residual but a relative $L_2$ error of 1.368. Gaussian-process surrogates were additionally evaluated using case-wise holdout tests on corrected Czochralski CFD parameter sweeps. The temperature-field error for the temperature sweep was approximately 6%, whereas the axial-velocity error for the crystal-rotation sweep was approximately 42%. These findings show that adaptive control can improve equation satisfaction while weakening other physical constraints. PINN training should therefore be evaluated using separate PDE, boundary-condition, and solution-error metrics rather than weighted total loss alone.

offered.title: S$^{2}$-PINN: Stochastic Separable Physics-Informed Neural Networks
offered.abstract: Uncertainty quantification (UQ) for random partial differential equations (PDEs) is ubiquitous in computational science and engineering. However, classical spectral solvers for this class of problems face the curse of dimensionality, and existing neural solvers often ignore the stochastic structure that makes moments and calibration tractable. We introduce a stochastic separable physics-informed neural network, dubbed S$^{2}$-PINN, that represents the solution $u(t,\mathbf{x},\mathbf{Z})$ of a random PDE with a learnable Gaussian spatial dictionary, Fourier temporal features, and a generalized polynomial chaos (gPC) stochastic basis, coupled by a low-rank Canonical Polyadic (CP) tensor decomposition core. The method is trained with a hybrid strong-form and gPC-projected residual loss. Our theoretical analysis establishes that the separable class is dense in $L^2$ under mild conditions, and the projected residual corresponds exactly to a stochastic Galerkin constraint. Furthermore, we show that mini-batch projection coefficients are logarithmically dependent on the number of gPC modes, and that the orthogonality penalty controls the conditioning of the learned spatial dictionary. Using four manufactured random PDE benchmarks, we show that S$^{2}$-PINN outperforms nine baselines in terms of mean and variance accuracy, as well as calibration, while using significantly fewer parameters. Further evaluations on non-manufactured Poisson and Darcy problems, a stochastic Navier--Stokes problem, a diffusion scaling study of higher random dimensions, and two stochastic inverse problems reveal the generalization capabilities of the proposed structure. Together, these results support stochastic separability as an effective design principle for physics-informed neural UQ. The code for the experiments can be found in https://github.com/DMax1314/s2pinn

offered.title: Puncture Evolution with Physics-Informed Neural Networks
offered.abstract: We investigate the application of physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) to solve the vacuum Einstein equations in spherical symmetry. Our neural network architecture is designed to solve the 1+1D moving-puncture evolution, by minimizing a loss that combines a data term, the Ricci tensor of the reconstructed spacetime, and the moving-puncture gauge conditions. It represents the lapse, the shift and the Z4c conformal variables $χ$ and $\widetildeγ_{rr}$, which remain regular at the puncture. We consider the evolution of a single, non-spinning black-hole in the puncture gauge and show that PINNs can interpolate numerical relativity (NR) data, predict its evolution, and reconstruct spacetime in regions where no data is provided. As an interpolant, the network provides a compact, differentiable representation of the NR data. Given only early-time and outer-boundary data, it evolves the puncture forward in time and reproduces the main features of the NR solution. Given only exterior data and no gauge condition, an ill-posed inverse problem, it recovers the interior of a Schwarzschild spacetime in coordinates of its own choosing, which we verify by learning the coordinate transformation to the Kerr--Schild form. Finally, we assess the strengths and limitations of PINNs for NR and outline their prospects for future applications.

offered.title: Gen-PINNs: Generative Adversarial Physics Informed Neural Networks for solving partial differential equations
offered.abstract: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) are a widely used data-free method for solving Partial Differential Equations (PDEs) using machine learning. With recent advances in Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), adversarial learning has shown strong capabilities for modeling complex data-driven problems; however, the use of GANs in deterministic physics-informed PDE solutions remains limited. In this work, we first identify limitations of standard PINNs for solving PDEs, including spectral bias, loss imbalance, and optimizer stagnation. We then propose Generative Adversarial Physics-Informed Neural Networks (Gen-PINNs), a unified deterministic residual-adversarial framework designed to improve data-free solutions of PDEs with sharp or shock-front behavior. The generator learns the underlying PDE solution using dynamically weighted physics-informed loss components, while separate discriminators evaluate complementary PDE residual features against ideal zero-residual states. The framework further develops and adapts several methodological components, including a Fourier representation for resolving high-frequency spatial content, an orthonormal spectral diagnostic for quantifying frequency-dependent solution errors, and a modified gradient-based dynamic weighting system for physics, initial-condition, boundary-condition, and adversarial loss objectives. Gen-PINNs is tested against standard PINNs on nonlinear and higher-order PDEs, including the Burgers, Allen-Cahn, and Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equations. The results demonstrate substantial improvements in accuracy and convergence across sharp-front, stiff, and higher-order PDE solutions, highlighting the potential of deterministic residual-adversarial learning as an effective approach for solving challenging nonlinear PDEs.

offered.title: A mesh-based neural energy method for the simulation of heterogeneous composites
offered.abstract: Modeling heterogeneous materials remains a challenge for physics-informed neural networks such as the deep energy method (DEM). The DEM and its variants, here collectively referred to as the neural energy method (NEM), offer a differentiable variational framework. However, their conventional collocation-based implementation (C-NEM) often suffers from physically inadmissible displacement oscillations, integration errors, and high computational costs from automatic differentiation. This work introduces the mesh-based neural energy method (M-NEM), extending the NEM through a mesh-based discretization of the displacement field. By interpolating nodal displacements via shape functions, the M-NEM imposes a kinematic constraint that suppresses oscillations. Furthermore, the method replaces automatic differentiation with algebraic shape function derivatives for strain computation and employs high-order Gaussian quadrature for accurate energy integration. On a directly comparable benchmark problem, the M-NEM reduces stress errors by up to three orders of magnitude relative to the C-NEM while being one to two orders of magnitude faster. On two further benchmarks involving extreme stiffness contrasts, only the M-NEM converges. A comparative study of neural architectures reveals that radial basis function neural networks (RBFNNs) yield optimal performance within the M-NEM, resolving sharp gradients at material interfaces with higher accuracy than multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) with random Fourier feature (RFF) mapping and faster convergence than Kolmogorov-Arnold networks (KANs).

offered.title: Cova-PINN: Cross-Domain Conservation Physics-Informed Neural Network for Fluid-Solid Conjugate Heat Transfer in Complex Geometries
offered.abstract: Multi-domain physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) flexibly model medium-specific representations to solve fluid--solid conjugate heat transfer (CHT). However, standard multi-domain PINNs enforce governing equations and interface conditions on separately sampled domain supports, which can yield plausible temperature fields but inaccurate end-to-end energy transfer and outlet temperatures. We propose Cova-PINN, a multi-domain PINN framework that aligns conservation support with thermal interaction paths in complex geometries. Cova-PINN jointly optimizes cross-domain composite control-volume balances at the local scale and paired-wall closure at the global exchanger scale. We evaluate Cova-PINN on four triply periodic minimal surface (TPMS) heat exchangers and a geometrically distinct DualMS design against CHT-specific, optimization-oriented, and complex-geometry PINN baselines under a common protocol. Relative to the closest baseline, MUSA-PINN-CHT, Cova-PINN reduces average outlet-temperature and device-level closure errors across the four TPMS topologies by $37.7\%$ and $60.2\%$, respectively, while also improving full-field and heat-duty accuracy, with consistent gains on DualMS.

overviews.overview: This period’s PINN work concentrated on making the physics prior structurally harder to violate, either by changing the training schedule or by embedding the right operator geometry into the model. For long-time PDEs, causality-enforced evolutional networks split time into nonoverlapping subintervals, trained sequentially from the initial step, and reported better accuracy with less memory and compute than standard PINNs on several problems [2610.04405]. On the optimization side, SoftServe extends quasi-Newton updates to PINNs with positive-definite curvature estimates and GPU-friendly Newton-Schulz iterations, and it is reported to beat Adam, Muon, and SOAP on ill-conditioned tasks including a 136M-parameter physics-informed diffusion model [2610.02182]. In parallel, conformal and multiphysics formulations kept pushing accuracy by enforcing the right constraints, from exact symmetries to temperature-dependent properties [2610.04082] [2610.01874].

picks.hook: Best starting point for the long-time-dynamics thread: it attacks the core PINN failure mode by enforcing temporal causality through subinterval networks and sequential training, with explicit claims of lower memory and better accuracy.

Worth reading for the optimizer angle: it gives a scalable quasi-Newton recipe with positive-definite curvature estimates and reports gains on PINNs and a 136M-parameter physics-informed diffusion model.

offered.title: PINNs for N=2* holography
offered.abstract: Can a holographic theory be reconstructed from its equation of state? We investigate this question using physics-informed neural networks in the bosonic-mass sector of the Pilch--Warner model. We first validate the PINN approach against an analytic solution encoding the leading high-temperature corrections to the conformal equation of state. We then reconstruct nonlinear black-brane geometries and the scalar potential using thermodynamics, ultraviolet asymptotics, Ward identities, and horizon regularity. Independent solutions of the bulk Einstein-scalar equations demonstrate that accurately reproducing thermodynamics with a trained PINN does not guarantee an accurate reconstruction of the scalar potential. High-precision knowledge of the high-temperature equation of state constrains nonlinear interactions in the bulk scalar potential. Fixing the cubic coupling to its exact PW value, motivated by this high-temperature extraction, reduces the maximum sampled error in the reconstructed scalar self-interactions by a factor of $\sim 15$ compared with constraining only the bulk scalar mass. Adding knowledge of the bulk viscosity of the gauge theory plasma further reduces this error by an additional factor of $\sim 13$, with independent forward solutions reproducing the bulk viscosity within $0.09\%$.

offered.title: Physics-informed random neural architectures on compact boundaryless multiply connected manifolds for random-operator models in machine learning and uncertainty quantification
offered.abstract: We introduce stochastic physics-informed neural networks (SPINNs) for stochastic boundary-value problems (SBVPs) with random operators. The method enforces physics through a structural probabilistic coupling: a common Gaussian stochastic germ drives both the SBVP random operator and a manifold-based stochastic neural architecture. The stochastic neural network is non-feedforward and intrinsically random. A latent Gaussian field and an inhomogeneous Poisson point process on a compact, boundaryless, multiply connected manifold generate random neuron locations, geodesically local sparse connectivity, and a sparse random weight matrix, all governed by a low-dimensional hyperparameter. For deterministic inputs, the network output is random and can represent non-Gaussian random operators. Training is performed in observation space: SBVP simulations produce random observables, while the SNN defines a predictive conditional probability density function. The supervised objective combines data fidelity, through negative log-likelihood, with a cross-entropy alignment term relative to the SBVP-induced conditional distribution. The resulting target is a convex mixture of observation-induced and SBVP-induced distributions, with a dimensionless parameter controlling robustness to model--data mismatch. The shared stochastic germ yields common-random-numbers Monte Carlo estimators and reduced-variance gradients. The method uses only evaluations of the SBVP solution mapping, without differentiating or modifying it, and avoids PDE-residual or boundary-penalty losses. A stochastic elliptic problem on a periodic cylindrical surface illustrates the approach in SBVP-consistent and SBVP-misspecified regimes. A generalized-posterior formulation is also outlined for hyperparameter inference and posterior averaging without per-query reoptimization.

offered.title: Utilizing Neural Networks for Solving Functional Renormalization Group Flow Equations
offered.abstract: A novel physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) based approach for solving functional renormalization group flow equations is presented. We investigate the finite temperature phase transition in $O(N)$ models without relying on the large-$N$ approximation, which was used in earlier attempts with similar methods. We argue that these previous solutions cannot easily be generalized for more complex symmetries, and hence our approach can provide new insight. Our technique relies on a series of ansätze that combines the small- and large-field approximation schemes with a neural network, leading to a highly accurate approximation over the entire field range. We compare the PINNs approach with traditional grid-based Runge-Kutta results and show that the network can successfully learn the temperature, field, and scale dependencies of the effective potential in the local potential approximation.

offered.title: PDE-PFN: Prior-Data Fitted Neural PDE Solver
offered.abstract: Motivated by the success of large language models (LLMs) with broad generalizability and robustness to noisy or unreliable pre-training data, we explore in-context prediction of PDE solution fields using approximate pre-training data. In addition, inspired by the posterior predictive mean-based inference mechanism of the in-context learning in prior-data fitted networks (PFNs), we propose PDE-PFN, a prior-data fitted neural solver that approximates the posterior predictive mean of PDE solutions via in-context learning. PDE-PFN builds on a PFN architecture with self- and cross-attention mechanisms of Transformer and is pre-trained on noisy approximate solutions generated by physics-informed neural networks, serving as diverse but not necessarily exact priors. Through experiments on a range of two-dimensional PDEs, we demonstrate that PDE-PFN achieves empirical generalization across heterogeneous equations, robustness under noisy priors, and zero-gradient-update in-context inference capability. PDE-PFN achieves competitive or improved predictive accuracy relative to the evaluated baselines while supporting flexible context and query representations.

offered.title: Sequential Learning-Based Physics-Informed Neural Network Modeling for Parameter Estimation on a Power Converter
offered.abstract: A staged physics-informed neural network (PINN) is proposed for identifying the inductance, capacitance and parasitic resistances of a DC buck converter from time-domain data. Gradients are released in the order of L to C to rL to rC, a sequence derived from sensitivity analysis. The five-stage schedule recovers L and C to within 5% and the series ESR to 10%, while a three-stage variant attains the same accuracy 11% faster. An 84 factorial sweep confirms that the trained PINN remains accurate for simultaneous 8% perturbations of all four components, achieving a waveform RMSE of 2.6 x 10-2 over 5 ms-an order-of-magnitude better than a simultaneous-training baseline.

offered.title: AI Meets Turbulence Modeling: Complex Systems Perspective
offered.abstract: Despite widespread enthusiasm, applying artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) to turbulence modeling has yielded only modest progress, primarily due to a lack of situation-aware deployment. Data-driven Reynolds-averaged Navier--Stokes (ML-RANS) closures frequently fail to generalize across diverse flow regimes, while scale-resolving simulations (SRS) remain computationally prohibitive. As a result, ML-RANS is often misapplied outside its domain of validity, and ML-SRS is unnecessarily deployed on flows fully amenable to RANS. To guide optimal AI/ML deployment, we propose a turbulence taxonomy map parameterized by degrees of freedom ($Re$) and the degree of non-equilibrium ($SK/ε$). By applying Weaver's well-recognized complexity framework, we classify turbulence into distinct physical regimes. This categorization identifies where local ML-RANS surrogates can generalize, clarifies where explicit scale resolution is physically mandatory, and highlights where physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) are most effective. Ultimately, this perspective establishes a physics-grounded framework for the flow-aware, successful deployment of AI/ML in turbulence.

offered.title: Conformalized Physics-Informed Weak Regression for Parameter Estimation in Epidemic Models
offered.abstract: Compartment models of infectious diseases are often linear in coefficients that are physical parameters or products or ratios of them. We exploit this with closed-form least squares and equip the estimates with distribution-free uncertainty. Physics-informed regression (PIR) fits the parameters to finite-difference derivatives of the data; we introduce physics-informed weak regression (PIWR), which integrates the model in time instead, needs no derivatives of the data, estimates the initial state jointly and is high-order accurate. To quantify uncertainty we wrap both estimators in split conformal prediction, with a calibration population generated by the physics-based model itself, giving simultaneous intervals for all parameters with a finite-sample coverage guarantee. A residual-adaptive factor, computed without ground truth, scales the intervals to each data set (PIWR-RACC). On the eleven benchmark models of disease-informed neural networks (DINNs), PIWR or PIR-FD6 is one to four orders of magnitude more accurate than the reported DINN results wherever the sampling resolves the dynamics, in about a millisecond per fit instead of minutes to hours of training, and the 90% intervals achieve 87-92% coverage in all 88 settings. On the S3I3R model of the original PIR study, PIWR lowers the reported PIR errors by about three orders of magnitude. On real data from the 1978 boarding-school influenza outbreak, a variable-projection variant gives calibrated 95% intervals that overlap those of a Bayesian analysis. On a time-varying transmission benchmark, a B-spline expansion of beta(t) keeps PIR and PIWR linear; they are more accurate than physics-informed neural networks in three of four cases and comparable in the noisiest, with simultaneous bands for beta(t). The complete conformal calibration takes less than two minutes for every benchmark.

offered.title: The importance of tensor handling and implementation of physics-informed DeepONets
offered.abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) reduce or eliminate the need for large labelled datasets by enforcing governing equations during training. Physics-informed Deep Operator Networks (PI-DeepONets) extend this approach to learning solution operators, enabling rapid prediction across families of problems. Despite these advantages, we show that their application to higher-dimensional problems remains limited by the computational cost of training. To address this issue, we propose a modified PI-DeepONet architecture that reduces this cost by removing redundancy in how the Branch network processes input functions across collocation points. The proposed formulation is mathematically equivalent to the original architecture but reduces input tensor sizes and the number of Branch network evaluations. We analyse the computational complexity of both architectures and derive theoretical scaling laws for training time with respect to the number of collocation points and input functions. The proposed architecture is evaluated on 1D, 2D, and 3D linear advection problems. In all cases, it achieves comparable predictive accuracy to the original PI-DeepONet while consistently reducing training time. In 2D experiments, a maximum speed-up of $3.75\times$ is observed, with empirical training-time scaling agreeing with the predicted linear dependence on collocation points and input functions. Furthermore, training a 3D model on an NVIDIA A100 GPU is only feasible using the proposed architecture, as the original formulation exceeds memory limits. These results demonstrate that careful consideration of how PI-DeepONets are implemented can yield substantial gains, enhancing the practical performance of PI-DeepONets and enabling their application to otherwise intractable physics-informed learning problems.

offered.title: A Multi-Agent LLM System for Automated Tuning of Specialized Neural Network Models
offered.abstract: Many machine learning approaches are two-level: an expert selects a class of methods, within this class the choice of key components is critical and usually manual. This paper addresses the automatic tuning of these components and proposes a framework transferable across models of different nature. The multi-agent large language model (LLM) framework has three roles---analyst, coder, and recorder~---with an experiment log and a sandboxed execution environment. Unlike systems that optimize the entire ML script or search architectures in a discrete space, the framework operates over an open but semantically narrow space: the agent generates code only for the specified components, leaving the overall network structure unchanged. The approach is validated in two directions: tuning a classification spiking neural network with correlation learning, and solving high-order differential equations with Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINN). Across five tasks---spiking classification on MNIST and Digits, and boundary-value problems for the generalized nonlinear Schrödinger equation (GNLSE) and Kuramoto--Sivashinsky (KS) equations---the agent outperforms the baselines: classification accuracy is 13 percentage points (MNIST) and 6 percentage points (Digits) higher; the error against the analytical single-soliton solution is reduced approximately 2491-fold; the invariant-preservation error drops approximately 325-fold in the selected GNLSE run with a Gaussian perturbation and by more than 100-fold on average over repeated initializations; and the mass drift drops 14-fold for the KS problem with a Gaussian perturbation. The framework thus tunes key components on tasks of different nature without changing its internal structure.

offered.title: Energy-Guided Learning for Heat Equation with Noisy Source: Optimal Estimation and Generalization Bounds
offered.abstract: Data and the governing partial differential equations (PDEs) of continuous-time dynamical systems provide rich structure for statistical learning. A central challenge is how to integrate data with PDE constraints in a principled way to improve generalization. In this paper, we characterize the statistical estimation and generalization properties of learning solutions to the heat equation with a noisy source function from finite, randomly sampled data. We first derive a novel variational formulation, which we characterize as the minimizer of loss function for an energy regularized and ellipticity debiased Sobolev regression. By formulating the learning task as a supervised problem over space-time domains under physically meaningful norms, our approach goes beyond the traditional supervised learning framework by effectively leveraging \emph{auxiliary data}---samples of the source function of the heat equation---to design a \emph{physics-informed energy regularization}. Our analysis reveals that learning in linear parabolic PDEs exhibits intrinsic anisotropy between spatial and temporal regularity, in sharp contrast to the static elliptic problems, leading to fundamentally different estimation and generalization behaviors. Specifically, we derive non-asymptotically rate-optimal estimation errors, as well as generalization error, which explicitly capture the interplay among temporal sampling, spatial resolution, and solution smoothness. Our numerical experiments demonstrate substantial orders of magnitude of reduction in testing errors against various physics-informed neural network methods on various parabolic and hyperbolic PDEs.

offered.title: Beyond Time Induction: Structured Conditional Neural Solvers for Parametric Stochastic-Volatility Pricing
offered.abstract: Physics-informed neural networks provide a flexible framework for learning parametric PDE solution families without labeled data, yet preserving accurate derivatives across heterogeneous regimes remains challenging. Structured neural solvers offer compact representations, but restrictive conditional parameterizations can limit adaptation across the solution family. We introduce BeTINN, a structured conditional architecture extending time-induced modulation through multi-directional time-parameter conditioning and a joint residual pathway. We evaluate BeTINN on the Heston stochastic-volatility PDE, a demanding parametric problem with mixed derivatives and economically relevant first- and second-order sensitivities. BeTINN improves joint accuracy across normalized option value and key sensitivity metrics relative to our baselines. Controlled ablations characterize the roles of its architectural components. We further find that validation physics loss is informative but does not fully determine differential fidelity, and that accurate solution values can coexist with localized derivative errors. These results support structured conditional adaptation and motivate derivative-aware evaluation when sensitivities are downstream quantities of interest.

offered.title: Neural Dimensional Analysis: Foundations of Dimensionless and Scale-Consistent Computation
offered.abstract: Modern Transformers rely on many scale-control mechanisms, including normalization, residual scaling, attention temperatures, loss weighting, and adaptive updates. To explain how these mechanisms maintain scale consistency, we introduce Neural Dimensional Analysis (NDA), a unified framework based on dimensional consistency. We define neural units that specify how tensors rescale and which quantities can be added, just as physical units do in physics. Our rules match residual units, nondimensionalize attention and gate inputs, combine losses across units, and convert gradient units into parameter units. We implement NDA through dimensionless Unit Violation Indices (UVI) for diagnosing scale mismatches within Transformers, a unit-consistent multi-loss objective, and the Gauge-Canonical Transformer (GCT) with normalized coordinates and orthogonalized residual additions. In language-model experiments spanning 51M to 1B parameters, GCT remains stable during training across a broad sixteenfold learning-rate range, outperforming Pre-LN, LLaMA-style, and QK-Norm in 124M validation loss at tuned learning rates. GCT's normalized residual stream also shows improved robustness to quantization. At 1B parameters, calibrated per-tensor int8 quantization increases GCT's validation loss by only 0.009 nats, compared with up to 5.51 nats for the baselines. Vision and physics-informed neural network experiments further confirm NDA's benefits beyond language modeling. These results establish dimensional consistency as a neural network design principle.

offered.title: AI-Assisted Tumor-Growth Law Discovery from Sparse Data: Refitting and LLM-Based Ranking
offered.abstract: Inferring tumor-growth laws from sparse, noisy observations requires more than accurate curve fitting. We study an AI-assisted workflow involving symbolic regression, mathematical admissibility checks, coefficient refitting, and large language model (LLM) ranking. Synthetic Gompertz data allow trajectory fit, forecasting, and recovery of the governing growth law to be assessed separately. A dense noiseless control recovers the generating family, but sparse noisy sampling frequently leads to alternative forms. Among retained candidates in the tested configurations, physics-informed neural network refitting often increases growth-law error, whereas classical nonlinear least squares usually reduces it. A separate exploratory analysis of archived LLM rankings shows no consistent improvement over selection by training error and identifies errors in mathematical reasoning. Plausible saturation, accurate trajectory fits, and convincing explanations can therefore coexist with incorrect growth laws. Mathematical validity and law recovery require evaluation alongside predictive performance.

overviews.overview: This period’s PINN work split between harder structural priors and more explicit uncertainty or conditioning. In holography, a PINN reconstructed black-brane geometries and scalar potentials from thermodynamics, UV asymptotics, Ward identities, and horizon regularity, but the authors show that matching the equation of state alone does not fix the bulk potential; pinning the cubic coupling to its exact value cut the maximum sampled self-interaction error by about 15x, and adding bulk-viscosity information cut it by another 13x while reproducing viscosity within 0.09% [2610.14461]. On the stochastic side, a manifold-based SPINN couples a common Gaussian germ to both random operators and random neuron locations, training on observation-space likelihoods plus distribution alignment to model non-Gaussian random operators with reduced-variance gradients [2610.14844].

picks.hook: Best starting point if you care about what physics data can and cannot identify: it quantifies when thermodynamics alone leaves the bulk potential underdetermined, and how much exact coupling and viscosity information tighten the reconstruction.

Start here for the new stochastic formulation: it turns the physics prior into a shared random germ and a manifold-based random architecture, with a likelihood-plus-alignment objective for random-operator learning.

offered.title: Low Residuals, Wrong Value: Learning the Viscosity Solution of Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs Equations with PINNs
offered.abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) and other residual-trained solvers judge a candidate solution by the size of its sampled PDE residual. For first-order Hamilton-Jacobi equations this is not sufficient: the same equation and boundary data admit Lipschitz almost-everywhere solutions that differ from the viscosity solution by $O(1)$ while violating the equation only on sets of measure zero. We study whether residual minimization selects such solutions in a fixed-horizon pursuit-evasion game whose Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs value function is known in closed form on the circle $S^1$ and on the flat tori $\mathbb{T}^{2}$ and $\mathbb{T}^{4}$. We train four neural parameterizations with ten seeds on each geometry, 120 runs in total. A standard network with periodic Fourier features converges to folded almost-everywhere solutions in all 30 runs: small residuals and the expected capture-layer gradient, yet values that are wrong over most of the domain. A network with periodicity imposed through the loss recovers the viscosity solution in one and two dimensions but becomes unreliable in four. Two parameterizations that receive the geodesic distance do substantially better: a single network fed the wrapped displacement and its distance recovers the viscosity solution in all 30 runs, while a minimum over periodic image charts succeeds in 27 of 30 and introduces a wrong-image failure mode. Finally, for the convex Hamiltonian considered here, we use the semiconcavity of the viscosity solution to build a mesh-free finite-difference test that needs only forward network evaluations; it detects the folded solutions and the harmful min-of-charts failures without access to the exact value function. A small sampled residual thus does not by itself validate a learned Hamilton-Jacobi solution; the parameterization and independent structural diagnostics can be essential for selecting the viscosity solution.

offered.title: HypoNet Nankai PS: rapid hypocenter determination for the Nankai Trough using physics-informed neural networks with three-dimensional P- and S-wave velocity models
offered.abstract: Rapid and accurate hypocenter determination based on three-dimensional (3D) seismic velocity models is essential for seismic monitoring in subduction zones, yet it remains computationally demanding. HypoNet Nankai, a hypocenter determination package that uses physics-informed neural network (PINN) travel-time inference for a realistic 3D P-wave velocity model of the Nankai Trough subduction zone, was designed to address this problem, but supported only P-wave arrival times. Here, we present HypoNet Nankai PS, which extends the framework to both P- and S-wave travel times. We first constructed an S-wave velocity model from the existing P-wave model using empirical conversion relations for marine sediments and the crust. Because the resulting S-wave velocity structure has lower velocities and therefore considerably steeper travel-time gradients, the original PINN training procedure designed for the P-wave velocity structure was insufficient. We therefore revised the training procedure by reconsidering the distribution of collocation points, the NN architecture, and the optimizer. Benchmark comparisons with the fast marching method showed that the revised approach substantially reduced the root-mean-square deviations for both P- and S-waves compared with the original algorithm. Recovery tests using synthetic earthquakes were also performed. When applied to 223 earthquakes recorded by DONET stations off the Kii Peninsula, the system yielded hypocenters generally consistent with the JMA catalog beneath the network, suggesting that the 3D velocity model captures travel-time variations accommodated by JMA's 1D model and station corrections. Farther seaward, the estimated hypocenters were substantially shallower than those in the JMA catalog and were located in the oceanic crust and uppermost mantle, consistent with previous relocations that used DONET data and 3D velocity models.

offered.title: Reconstruction of Magnetic Fields with a Physics-Informed Neural Network
offered.abstract: Accurate reconstruction of magnetic fields and their gradients is essential for assessing and controlling systematic effects in precision measurement experiments. We have developed a physics-informed neural network (PINN) method which reconstructs three-dimensional magnetic fields subject to the source-free Maxwell equations, $\nabla\cdot\mathbf{B}=0$ and $\nabla\times\mathbf{B}=\mathbf{0}$. In an extension of our previous work on PINN methods for reconstruction of magnetic fields in inaccessible interior regions via measurements at exterior locations, we now demonstrate the feasibility of applying PINN methods to the extraction of magnetic field gradient terms from discrete measurement points subject to constraints from Maxwell's equations.

offered.title: GeoDiv KAN Solver for Time Fractional Navier Stokes Equations on Complex Domains to Realistic CFD Reconstruction
offered.abstract: Scientific machine learning provides a promising framework for solving complex problems in science and engineering. Notably, physics informed neural networks (PINNs) have shown considerable potential for solving differential equations and modelling engineering systems. Solving time fractional Navier Stokes equations (TFNSEs) on complex domains is challenging due to temporal nonlocality, nonlinear flow dynamics, geometric complexity, and incompressibility constraints. To address these challenges, we propose a geometry gated, divergence-free Gaussian radial basis function Kolmogorov Arnold network (GeoDiv KAN). The proposed architecture uses geometry dependent feature gating and a streamfunction formulation to preserve incompressibility by construction. GeoDiv KAN is evaluated for the time fractional incompressible Navier-Stokes equations on square, circular, and star-shaped domains. Numerical experiments show that GeoDiv KAN achieves higher predictive accuracy than PINN, PIKAN, RBF KAN, and DF RBFKAN across the considered benchmark problems. To establish practical relevance, GeoDiv KAN is applied to two data driven CFD cases: unsteady flow past a circular cylinder using the \href{https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.5039610}{Zenodo dataset} and turbulent RANS flow through a complex U bend using the \href{https://huggingface.co/datasets/JDecke/ubend-cfd}{U-bend dataset}.

offered.title: Improved three component IVIM fitting using physics-informed neural network with multimodal spatial prior
offered.abstract: Purpose: To mitigate parameter degeneracy and improve robustness of IVIM fitting, a multimodal physics-informed neural network was developed to leverage anatomical information through the combined use of cross attention, selective spatial gating, and anatomy-weighted spatial prior. Methods: T1w and FLAIR anatomical images were co-registered to IVIM signal in native space and segmented by tissue type. The proposed Physics-Anchored Cross-attention Embedding network (PACE) encoded IVIM signals and their anatomical features in parallel branches, then integrated them via cross attention and spatial gating. An anatomy-weighted spatial prior further constrained signal reconstruction using anatomically similar neighboring voxels. PACE and its prior-guided variant were compared with two baseline deep neural networks (DNN and IVIM3C), least squares, non-negative least squares, and maximum a posteriori fitting models. All models were evaluated on signal and parameter reconstruction accuracy and lesion contrast fidelity using data generated from subjects drawn from the University of Rochester COVID cohort. Results: PACE variants demonstrated lower RMSE for all IVIM parameters except for Dmv. The anatomy-weighted spatial prior further reduced RMSE across all five parameters relative to the default PACE, with modest reductions in lesion contrast accuracy for fmv and fint. For in-vivo evaluation, PACE with spatial prior also showed the best signal reconstruction across all noise levels while maintaining good to excellent ICC. Conclusion: Multimodal anatomical information improved IVIM fitting accuracy and robustness, with selective spatial integration via cross attention, gating, and anatomy-weighted spatial prior. Keywords: intravoxel incoherent motion, physics-informed deep learning, diffusion MRI, multimodality fusion, attention mechanism

offered.title: Soliton Profiles in 1D: Enhanced Neural-Network Solvers and Constrained Deep Ritz Methods
offered.abstract: We develop and compare enhanced neural-network solvers for one-dimensional ground-state profiles, which are solutions of $$ Q^{\prime\prime}=bQ-γQ^{p},\quad Q>0,\quad p>1, \quad b, γ>0, $$ the stationary profile equation for the nonlinear Schrödinger, generalized Korteweg-de Vries, and nonlinear Klein-Gordon equations. Its explicit sech-type solutions serve as exact reference for error computation and benchmark hyperparameter selection. We improve on the standard Adam-trained physics-informed neural network (PINN) baseline by introducing higher-order optimization via Gauss-Newton/Levenberg-Marquardt and L-BFGS refinements, as well as Fourier-feature PINNs, and constrained Deep Ritz (DR) formulations. In DR approaches we introduce two new neural-network formulations, which implement two classical variational characterizations: a Nehari-constrained Deep Ritz method, in which the height is learned by projecting onto the Nehari/Pokhozhaev manifold, and a Weinstein Deep Ritz method, in which a normalized profile minimizes the Weinstein quotient. The Deep Ritz formulations perform best overall, in particular, the Weinstein variant gives the best error-runtime balance. The neural-network based solvers remain less accurate and efficient than classical Petviashvili iteration in 1D, however, the current study provides a proof of concept: the mesh-free formulation, non-reliance on exact profiles or the related features make them promising in higher dimensions and for more complicated nonlinearities and dispersive operators.

offered.title: Physics-informed Neural Networks Based on the Fokker-Planck Model for Rarefied Gas Flows
offered.abstract: Rarefied nonequilibrium flows are described by the Boltzmann equation, which can be solved using stochastic particle or deterministic methods. With advances in computing, data-assisted physics-informed neural networks have been widely used for flow prediction by combining governing equations with measured or computed data. Data-free PINNs do not require such training data and have been widely studied for continuum flows, but their application to rarefied flows remains limited. This study develops a data-free Fokker-Planck physics-informed neural network (FP-PINN) to describe rarefied nonequilibrium flows. The physics loss is constructed from the ellipsoidal statistical Fokker-Planck (ES-FP) equation using a velocity distribution function (VDF) closure and moment projection. The FP-PINN is evaluated for a steady one-dimensional Mach 10 normal shock. The FP-PINN results agree with the numerical ES-FP results, with errors below $1\%$. Compared with the particle ES-FP results, the FP-PINN predicts a sharper shock structure with errors up to $17\%$. This difference is attributed to the VDF closure and moment projection.

offered.title: PaPi: Parallel Picard-Duhamel Integration for Fast Neuro-Spectral Architectures
offered.abstract: Neuro-spectral architectures (NeuSA) are a class of physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) that have proven effective for solving time-dependent PDEs in the frequency domain. However, training and inference often rely on costly numerical integration of the learned vector field, typically using sequential Runge-Kutta time stepping, which limits temporal parallelism. We introduce PaPi, an integration scheme inspired by weakly nonlinear flows that enables time-Parallel inference through exponential integration and a Duhamel-Picard scheme. We show that the Duhamel-Picard iteration converges exponentially for all flows, and provide explicit error bounds that depend on how close the flow is to linear. Experiments show that PaPi accelerates training and inference by up to two orders of magnitude, achieving training times of under one second for low-dimensional PDE learning problems, while maintaining competitive predictive accuracy.

offered.title: Binary Black Hole Puncture Initial Data with Physics-Informed Neural Networks
offered.abstract: We present Pinndorama, a physics-informed neural network (PINN) code for solving the Hamiltonian constraint in the puncture formalism. The networks are trained solely on the governing equation and boundary conditions, without an analytical or perturbative guiding solution, with collocation points sampled in curvilinear coordinates. Training combines two optimization algorithms: an initial stage using adaptive moment estimation (Adam), followed by the self-scaled Broyden quasi-Newton method. We apply this approach to a spherically symmetric test problem with a known exact solution, axisymmetric binary punctures with unequal spins, and a fully three-dimensional GW150914-like configuration with unequal spins and orbital momenta. Comparisons with the NRPyElliptic solver yield relative $L^2$ errors of order $10^{-8}$ in axisymmetry and $10^{-5}$ in three dimensions. In addition, we reduce the hyperbolic-relaxation time in NRPyElliptic by a factor of approximately $4.6$ by training a parametric network that takes the puncture spin as input and provides a physics-informed initial guess to the solver. These results demonstrate that PINNs can provide accurate binary-puncture initial data and complement conventional elliptic solvers in numerical relativity.

offered.title: Fourier-Feature-Embedded Complex-Valued Physics-Informed Convolutional Residual Networks for Sparse and Gappy Noisy Flow-Field Reconstruction
offered.abstract: Reconstructing flow fields from sparse and noisy measurements becomes particularly challenging when data are completely absent from dynamically critical regions, such as the vortex-formation region of a wake. Conventional interpolation and numerical reconstruction methods generally require sufficient spatial or boundary information, while physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) can also face difficulties when sparse and noisy observations provide little or no supervision in the region of interest. To address this gap, we propose a Fourier-feature-embedded complex-valued physics-informed convolutional residual network (FCV-PICRN) for sparse, gappy, and noisy flow-field reconstruction. The framework integrates Fourier features for oscillatory and multiscale structures, complex-valued representations for coupled amplitude--phase learning, and convolutional residual blocks constrained by the Navier--Stokes equations. The method is first verified using the Taylor--Green vortex at $Re=100$ and then evaluated for the cylinder wake at $Re=100$. Three severe missing-data configurations are imposed in the dynamically sensitive wake: a large hole, a large truncation, and a plus-shaped gap extending in both streamwise and transverse directions. These gaps are further combined with additive Gaussian and multiplicative speckle noise. Despite having no supervised velocity data inside the excluded regions, FCV-PICRN reconstructs velocity, pressure, and vorticity with high structural similarity index (SSIM) and peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR), and remains robust under Gaussian noise up to $20\%$. Finally, for forced two-dimensional Kolmogorov turbulence with $5\%$ Gaussian noise, FCV-PICRN yields lower reconstruction errors than a conventional PINN. These results demonstrate robust physics-informed reconstruction of severely incomplete and noisy flows across laminar and turbulent regimes.

offered.title: PINN-LPCDD: Physics-Informed Neural Network with Learnable and Physically Consistent Domain Decomposition for Compressible Multi-Medium Flows
offered.abstract: The physics-informed neural network (PINN) faces significant challenges when solving compressible multi-medium flows, including the inability to locate interface positions, poor approximation of discontinuities, and difficulty in handling high-pressure-ratio problems between media with large stiffness differences. To address these issues, we propose PINN with Learnable and Physically Consistent Domain Decomposition (PINN-LPCDD), a framework that incorporates the sharp interface method (SIM) into PINNs for solving compressible multi-medium flows. Firstly, we design separate sub-networks for each medium with learnable parameters to automatically learn interface positions, so that the domain decomposition is physically consistent, and the contact discontinuity at the interface is naturally sharp. Secondly, the Euler equations with artificial viscosity are solved to enhance robustness when handling problems involving shock waves. Lastly, the scaling invariance of the Euler equations is exploited to facilitate the solution of high pressure ratio problems. Numerical experiments on air-air, air-helium, air-water, and air-R22 problems demonstrate the acceptable accuracy of the proposed method in simulating multi-medium flows.

offered.title: Neural Network Representation of Generalized Parton Distributions (NNGPD)
offered.abstract: Extracting generalized parton distributions (GPDs) from experimental observables, the convolution structures denoted as Compton form factors (CFFs), requires solving an intrinsic inverse problem. We presented results using NNGPD, a flexible regression method based on a physics-informed neural-network framework, for reconstructing GPDs using integral constraints -- including CFFs and Mellin moments -- and symmetry and endpoint constraints. The approach does not require pointwise training information on the underlying GPDs. Closure tests using pseudodata generated from a phenomenological model demonstrate the ability of the framework to reproduce the principal features of the underlying distributions across a range of kinematics. A Bayesian neural-network formulation is also introduced to address uncertainties associated with the reconstruction. Finally, we discussed a broader question in GPD phenomenology: whether the complete momentum-fraction dependence of GPDs is necessary to extract physical quantities such as partonic angular momentum. This motivates investigating approaches that infer Mellin moments directly from experimentally constrained CFFs, while quantifying the remaining ambiguities.

offered.title: A mixed leading variable physics-informed neural network for nonsmooth dynamics simulation in contact systems
offered.abstract: High-accuracy computation of nonsmooth dynamics is a challenging problem in systems with multiple frictional contacts. This study proposes a general physics-informed neural network framework, termed the mixed leading variable physics-informed neural network (MLV-PINN). By using the governing equations and contact-friction laws as physical constraints, this framework provides common solution approaches for computing nonsmooth dynamics not only in discrete systems but also in continuum systems. Specifically, the network represents accelerations, normal contact forces and friction margins as independent outputs and determines them simultaneously, without first reducing the dynamics to discrete velocity-impulse complementary subproblems. A composite physics-informed loss is constructed from the equations of motion in their original form, contact-friction complementary conditions and a friction-margin consistency relation. To improve stick-slip state identification during PINN optimisation, a mixed leading variable combining relative tangential velocity and acceleration is introduced to reformulate the tangential complementary conditions. Four benchmark simulations cover one-dimensional (1-D) nonsmooth dynamics involving single-contact stick-slip, 1-D nonsmooth dynamics involving multi-contact stick-slip, two-dimensional (2-D) nonsmooth dynamics with coupled normal contact-separation and tangential stick-slip, and 2-D nonsmooth dynamics in a continuum system involving moving contact on an elastic beam. Benchmark comparisons show substantial reductions in displacement and velocity errors relative to the corresponding conventional methods at large time steps. These results, together with an ablation study and tests involving friction-velocity slopes, long-time integration and loss weights, illustrate the computational accuracy and support the broad applicability of the proposed framework.

offered.title: Manifold-Informed Neural Networks for Low-Label ECG Electrolyte Inference
offered.abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) supervise on the residual of a known differential operator. Many high-stakes inference problems admit no such operator: clinical signals, behavioral measurements, materials properties. We introduce the Manifold-Informed Neural Network (MINN), a PINN-parallel paradigm that replaces the physics operator residual with a manifold operator residual: a discrete Poisson equation $\mathbf{L}_G \mathbf{H} = s_φ(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{m})$ on a $k$-nearest-neighbor graph in the learned latent space, with a learned, task-aware source. The construction is a structural parallel to PINNs (squared operator residual plus label data, in place of operator residual plus boundary data); the $s{=}0$ limit recovers the homogeneous Laplace equation $\mathbf{L}_G\mathbf{H}=\mathbf{0}$ (classical manifold regularization solves the same equation but minimizes the Dirichlet energy $\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{H}^\top\mathbf{L}_G\mathbf{H})$, a different penalty form). The source $s_φ$ takes input features and auxiliary metadata directly, breaking the homogeneous smoothness prior that limits classical Laplacian penalties; gated Feature-wise Linear Modulation separately fuses metadata into the prediction branch. We evaluate MINN on three-class classification of potassium, calcium, and magnesium from 12-lead ECGs in MIMIC-IV-ECG, against twelve baselines spanning supervised and tabular methods, ECG foundation models, and manifold/graph approaches. MINN attains the highest K$^+$ Macro-F1 of 0.61 (best baseline 0.55), with consistent gains on Ca$^{2+}$ and Mg$^{2+}$ and a 31% relative improvement at 1% labeled data. Six targeted ablations show that the inhomogeneous Poisson formulation, not graph smoothing alone, drives the gain.

overviews.overview: This period’s PINN work is split between failure modes and domain-specific fixes. For Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs problems, residual minimization can drive the PDE residual near zero while converging to folded almost-everywhere solutions with values wrong over most of the domain; on a pursuit-evasion benchmark, a standard Fourier-feature network failed in all 30 runs, while feeding geodesic distance recovered the viscosity solution in all 30 runs, and a chart-based periodic model succeeded in 27 of 30 [2610.27193]. In seismology, extending travel-time PINNs from P-waves to both P and S waves required redesigning collocation, architecture, and optimization because the S-wave gradients were steeper; the revised system reduced RMS deviations against fast marching and worked on 223 earthquakes [2610.27561]. Other papers pushed PINNs into magnetic-field reconstruction from Maxwell constraints [2610.23691] and time-fractional Navier-Stokes on complex domains with a geometry-gated, divergence-free KAN that outperformed PINN baselines and CFD reconstructions [2610.30179].

picks.hook: Shows a concrete PINN pathology—tiny residuals with the wrong viscosity solution—and tests three parameterizations, including one that succeeds in all 30 runs.
A practical 3D travel-time PINN upgrade: it adds S-wave support, explains why the old training failed, and reports improved RMS errors plus 223-event application results.

offered.title: Physics Informed Neural Networks for Solving the Drift-Diffusion Equations
offered.abstract: The drift-diffusion equations are the fundamental building block for the modeling, design, and optimization of modern semiconductor devices. Solutions of the drift-diffusion equations rarely give way to analytical forms, and exhibit strong nonlinearity, with the solutions ranging over several orders of magnitude. These attributes have led to research into numerical solvers, and while many commercial Technology Computer Aided Design (TCAD) packages now exist, they may require long simulation times, exhibit sensitivity to initial guesses, and rely on mesh generation. Further, these solvers are not well suited for inverse problems where the design parameters of a device are retrieved from its desired functional characteristics. To address all these challenges, this work demonstrates the usage of Physics Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) for the solution of the drift-diffusion equations with errors comparable to traditional simulation software using advanced training techniques to solve problems beyond the well-behaved equilibrium regime. For this study, we specifically choose an abrupt PN-junction in both one and two dimensions that features extreme gradients of the carrier concentrations at the Ohmic contacts and an abrupt discontinuity in the doping profile. Using the proposed PINN architecture, we are able to retrieve accurate results for all observables under all bias conditions. Additionally, we apply the PINN solver towards the inverse problem of retrieving doping profiles directly from desired electric field distributions or electrostatic potentials under non-zero applied biases. Our work establishes a powerful PINNs-based approach for semiconductor device modeling with the ability to solve inverse problems under non-equilibrium conditions for microelectronics research and discovery.

offered.title: Sensitivity-Guided Parameter Estimation of Bubbly Liquid via a Nonlinear Wave Equation and Physics-InformedNeuralNetworks
offered.abstract: Interactions between ultrasound and microbubbles underlie a range of biomedical and industrial applications, yet predicting how the physical parameters of the medium and bubbles govern nonlinear wave propagation remains difficult. This study proposes a parameter estimation framework that combines a Korteweg-de Vries-Burgers (KdVB) equation, describing weakly nonlinear wave propagation in a bubbly liquid, with a physics-informed neural network (PINN). The contributions are threefold. First, the PINN reproduces the reference solution of the governing equation in the forward problem, with a near-zero prediction error at the initial time that confirms the initial condition is enforced exactly as intended. Second, prior to inverse estimation, a sensitivity analysis is introduced that quantifies, at both the coefficient and solution levels, how each of eight physical parameters influences the KdVB equation, allowing the expected difficulty of estimating each parameter to be assessed in advance. Third, based on this assessment, single-parameter inverse estimation is performed for seven of the eight parameters using the PINN. Liquid viscosity, bubble initial radius, liquid density, sound speed, and liquid pressure are estimated with errors of 0.8-2.1%, the polytropic exponent converges only partially, and the surface tension coefficient cannot be estimated at all, consistent with the sensitivity analysis. These results establish a general framework for identifying and estimating the physical parameters governing nonlinear wave propagation in bubbly liquids from observed waveform data.

offered.title: Regional accuracy of physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) for recirculation in a deep lid-driven cavity
offered.abstract: Deep lid-driven cavities contain strong motion beneath the lid and much weaker recirculation at depth, so agreement in bulk velocity is an incomplete assessment of a computed flow. We examine data-free physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) for steady, two-dimensional incompressible flow in a cavity of depth-to-width ratio five at Reynolds numbers 100, 250, 500 and 1000. An established hard-constrained streamfunction formulation is combined with prescribed regional collocation, transferred initialization, and selected residual-scaling and envelope variants. Independent spectral/$hp$ calculations with the same Gaussian-regularized lid provide the reference fields. For a cavity of depth-to-width ratio $D/W=5$ at Reynolds numbers $\mathrm{Re}=100$, 250, 500, and 1000, evaluation on a common $121\times605$ grid gives interior relative velocity discrepancies of 5.130\%--7.850\%. Over the same cases, floor-region relative velocity discrepancies remain below 5\%, with absolute RMS discrepancies ranging from $1.255\times10^{-10}U$ to $2.332\times10^{-9}U$, where $U$ is the lid-velocity scale. In a separate $161\times801$ assessment at $\Rey=1000$, the refined workflow lowers interior velocity discrepancy from 5.624\% to 2.658\% and gauge-aligned pressure RMS discrepancy from $2.793\times10^{-3}$ to $1.167\times10^{-3}ρU^2$. The improvements compare accumulated training workflows and do not isolate regional sampling. Configuration rankings depend on both region and observable. These finite-budget comparisons establish where the retained workflows agree with the reference and where rotational-field discrepancies remain substantial.

offered.title: Physics Informed Neural Network for Multi-dimensional Turbulent Self-gravitating Flows
offered.abstract: Molecular clouds exhibit complex, multi-scale dynamics driven by the interplay of turbulence, self-gravity, and gas pressure. Modelling these systems with conventional grid-based methods becomes increasingly expensive as spatial resolution and dimensionality increase. Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) offer a mesh-free alternative by incorporating the governing equations directly into the training objective, but their ability to model realistic turbulent self-gravitating flows remains largely unexplored. We apply PINNs to isothermal molecular clouds initialized with astrophysically motivated turbulent velocity fields, considering subsonic and supersonic evolution in two and three dimensions. We benchmark the predicted density and velocity fields against the finite-volume code Athena++. PINNs accurately recover the global evolution of the flow over multiple free-fall times across turbulent realizations, Mach numbers, and dimensionalities. Their training cost also exhibits weak dependence on spatial resolution, increasing by less than 25% from 128^3 to 1024^3 in our experiments. These results demonstrate that PINNs can model substantially more realistic self-gravitating turbulent flows than previously explored and provide a promising complementary framework for studying these systems.

offered.title: Hybrid-time PINNs: Discontinuity-Aware Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Learning Hybrid Dynamical Systems
offered.abstract: Hybrid dynamical systems flow continuously but jump at discrete events. Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) fit data while enforcing known dynamics, but a single network is smooth in time and cannot model these jumps. We show that the more closely a PINN follows a jump, the larger its physics loss must be. We propose hybrid-time PINNs (HT-PINNs), which assign one network to each flow interval of the hybrid time domain and train the networks jointly with the jump times and the unknown parameters. The number of jumps and the sequence of modes are found by enumeration. HT-PINNs recover the number of jumps and the restitution coefficient of a bouncing ball. In a MuJoCo simulation of robotic disassembly, where a robot pulls a press-fitted pin out of a housing through a spring, HT-PINNs find the number of jumps and the sequence of modes, and estimate the static and kinetic friction coefficients with small errors of 0.1% and 1.7%.

offered.title: Physics-Informed Neural Networks vs U-Net: Application to thermal dust emission recovery in the microwave
offered.abstract: Galactic thermal dust emission is the dominant foreground contaminant of the cosmic microwave background (CMB) at frequencies above 100 GHz, and its accurate separation is essential for current and future CMB experiments. Deep learning methods, in particular convolutional architectures such as the U-Net, have demonstrated strong performance for CMB component separation, but typically operate as purely data-driven models with no explicit enforcement of the physical laws governing the emission they reconstruct. In this work, we present a Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) that embeds the Modified Black Body (MBB) spectral model as a hard, differentiable architectural constraint, and we compare it against a standard U-Net baseline trained under an identical pipeline. Both architectures are trained on realistic simulated Planck HFI patches at four frequencies (143, 217, 353 and 545 GHz) and evaluated on a shared validation set as well as on three independent Galactic dust realizations from the PySM phenomenological dust models named D4, D7 and D10. We find that both networks achieve comparable reconstruction quality across all evaluated datasets, with a Structural Similarity Index Measure consistently above 0.96 and a fitted angular power-spectrum spectral index that agrees with the input to within 1% in every region. Embedding the physical constraint in the PINN does not measurably degrade reconstruction accuracy relative to the unconstrained U-Net, while additionally guaranteeing that every predicted output corresponds to a thermodynamically admissible physical configuration. These results establish the physics-informed formulation as a viable methodological alternative for dust component separation, providing physical interpretability without a trade-off in reconstruction fidelity.

offered.title: A Deep Learning-Driven Operator Splitting Scheme for Free Boundary Problems: An Application to American Option Pricing in Incomplete Markets
offered.abstract: This paper proposes a deep learning-driven operator splitting scheme for high-dimensional free-boundary problems, with American option pricing as a representative application. In a market with proportional transaction costs, a stochastic liquidity risk with an empirically validated nonlinear drift based on S&P 500 data, and two-factor stochastic volatility, the pricing problem takes the form of a five-dimensional highly nonlinear variational inequality. The proposed scheme decomposes this variational inequality at each time layer into an elliptic continuation equation approximated by a physics-informed neural network and a closed-form projection step enforcing the early-exercise constraint. A conditional $\ell^\infty$ stability bound is derived under stated resolvent and Lipschitz assumptions. The scheme is validated against finite-difference and least-squares Monte Carlo benchmarks, and both the option prices and the learned exercise boundary show close agreement with the reference solutions. Sensitivity analyses with respect to the key model parameters are also reported.

offered.title: QD-PINN:A Physics-Informed Neural Network Approach to Bayesian Quickest Detection in High-Dimensional Diffusions
offered.abstract: Quickest detection problems (QDPs) arise in a wide range of applications. However, the complementarity structure of the associated variational inequalities poses substantial challenges for traditional numerical methods, particularly in high-dimensional settings. We propose a PINN-based framework for estimating the optimal stopping boundary in QDPs with high-dimensional diffusion processes and spatial dependence, while overcoming the curse of dimensionality. Theoretically, we establish a novel equivalence between the free-boundary PDE and an infinite-dimensional stochastic optimization problem, rigorously justifying the use of finite-dimensional neural networks to approximate the true solution. Furthermore, we assess the robustness of the proposed framework by quantifying uncertainty in the learned stopping boundaries using deep ensembles and Monte Carlo dropout. The results show low variability across independent training runs and stochastic forward passes, indicating stable and consistent boundary estimates. We also compare our PINN results with reference numerical solutions where available and find close agreement.

offered.title: Physics-informed neural network (PINN) approximations of capillary menisci in polygonal channels
offered.abstract: In a zero-gravity cylindrical container, a meniscus can span a square or equilateral-triangular cross-section only at contact angles at or above the respective Concus-Finn critical angles of 45 degrees and 60 degrees. We study strong-form physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) across these thresholds under fixed collocation and optimization budgets. Classical capillary flux balance yields a lower bound on the combined interior and wall residual loss for arbitrary positive sampling densities. In the tested nonexistence regime, several degrees below the critical angles, independently evaluated network losses are 1.6-1.9 times this bound. A polynomial least-squares comparison supports the same geometric interpretation. The PINNs still return smooth graphs with finite axial extent, even though the prescribed equilibrium problem has no spanning graph solution. Their small interior residuals coexist with wall-flux deficits near corners, where adjoining contact-angle conditions demand more flux than a finite-slope graph can supply. Residuals vary on both sides of the critical angle, while the bound tends uniformly to zero at threshold for fixed wall weight. These results give a geometric scale for interpreting the computed loss and locate the incompatibility that a small interior residual can conceal.

offered.title: Inherent Failure Modes of Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Buoyancy-Driven Flow: Role of Non-Dimensionalization in Network Training
offered.abstract: We investigate the influence of non-dimensionalization on the trainability and accuracy of physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) for buoyancy-driven flows. Using a differentially heated square cavity at $\mathrm{Pr}=0.71$ and $\mathrm{Ra}=10^3$--$10^5$, we compare thermal-diffusive and free-fall velocity scalings under identical training conditions. The free-fall scaling, with a unit buoyancy coefficient, achieves errors below 1.1\% in the mean Nusselt number for $\mathrm{Ra}\le10^4$, whereas the diffusive scaling, with a buoyancy coefficient of $\mathrm{Ra}\,\mathrm{Pr}$, produces errors of 157--650\% and diverges at $\mathrm{Ra}=10^5$. We identify a coefficient-induced gradient imbalance, with the dominant buoyancy-related contribution to the loss gradient scaling as $(\mathrm{Ra}\,\mathrm{Pr})^2$, and confirm it through direct gradient measurements. Neither sparse-data supervision nor adaptive loss weighting resolves the training difficulties under the tested conditions. For unsteady convection, the free-fall PINN accurately predicts long-time heat transfer but fails to capture the transient Nusselt-number overshoot. These findings establish non-dimensionalization as an important design consideration for improving PINN trainability in buoyancy-driven flows.

offered.title: Cautious Conflict-Free Inverse Gradient Methods
offered.abstract: Partial differential equations (PDEs) are indispensable tools for modeling complex phenomena in physics and engineering. Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) have emerged as a powerful alternative to traditional numerical solvers by directly incorporating physical constraints into neural network loss functions. Despite their advantages, PINN training requires multi-objective optimization, which often leads to significant gradient conflicts among boundary, initial, and residual loss terms. The Conflict-Free Inverse Gradient (ConFIG) method addresses these conflicts; however, integrating ConFIG with adaptive optimizers such as Adam introduces a critical vulnerability: the conflict-free direction generated by ConFIG is further processed by the optimizer, and the resulting weight update may no longer be conflict-free with respect to the task gradients. To address this issue, Cautious ConFIG is proposed as a concise three-line extension to the ConFIG algorithm that empirically restores the conflict-freeness guarantee prior to the weight update. The method is evaluated on three PINN benchmarks: the 1D Viscous Burgers' equation, the 1D Nonlinear Schrödinger equation, and the 2D Kovasznay flow. Experimental results demonstrate consistent performance improvements over the standard ConFIG baseline. Additionally, the stabilizing effect of cautious masking and its reaction to conflict severity, task number, and optimizer lag are investigated using a simple toy system.

offered.title: A Physics-Informed Neural Network for Geodesic Computation and Visualization of Geodesic Spheres on Riemannian Manifolds
