offered.title: Construction of DAE solver Rodas4PW and numerical test examples with Rosenbrock and W-methods in OrdinaryDiffEqRosenbrock.jl
offered.abstract: This paper compares various Rosenbrock and Rosenbrock W-methods. To achieve this, some methods implemented in the Julia package OrdinaryDiffEqRosenbrock.jl are selected and benchmarked using test examples. The test examples include stiff ODE problems as well as differential-algebraic equations. In addition to the already known methods, the new W-method Rodas4PW is introduced and included in the tests.

offered.title: Asymptotic Robustness of HDG Schemes for the Convection-Diffusion Equation
offered.abstract: The convection-diffusion problem has been studied extensively as an important model for convection-dominated problems. The problem becomes more challenging when the convecting velocity is no longer Lipschitz and merely has Sobolev regularity. In this paper, we use Boyer's extension of the DiPerna--Lions theory for the transport equation to study the vanishing diffusion limit of discretizations of the convection-diffusion equation with Sobolev velocity. In the case of flux-adapted boundary conditions, we prove that a continuous Galerkin discretization converges strongly to the renormalized solution of the transport equation as the diffusion coefficient and mesh size go to zero, without requiring any relationship between them. We refer to this unconditional strong convergence as asymptotic robustness. In the case of Dirichlet boundary conditions, we use the renormalization theory and barrier arguments to prove that a piecewise constant hybridizable discontinuous Galerkin scheme is asymptotically robust, while the continuous Galerkin scheme may fail to converge. Our results indicate that the asymptotic robustness of schemes for the convection-diffusion problem depends on the realization of the boundary conditions as opposed to internal layers.

overviews.overview: This period centers on two themes: explicit time stepping that still respects gradient-flow structure, and parallel or operator-level reformulations that expose more hardware concurrency. For stiff Allen–Cahn and Cahn–Hilliard dynamics, stabilized explicit Runge–Kutta schemes of RKL/RKG type enlarge the stability region enough to avoid implicit solves; with Strang splitting they prove a 1D maximum principle for Allen–Cahn and energy dissipation in all dimensions, and the authors also derive new first-order stabilized variants plus a new eigenvalue estimate for second-order RKG [2611.16238]. On the algorithmic side, a Broyden-based quasi-Newton method uses diagonal-plus-low-rank Jacobian blocks from trajectory secants, avoids automatic differentiation, and can recover the exact trajectory in finitely many steps under compressed scan [2611.13523].

picks.hook: Best entry point for the period’s numerical-analysis core: it shows how fully explicit stabilized RK schemes can handle stiff phase-field PDEs while still proving maximum-principle and energy-dissipation properties.
Worth reading for the solver-design angle: it turns nonlinear state-space evaluation into a parallel root-finding problem with low-rank Broyden updates and finite-step recovery guarantees.

pairs.title: Improved three component IVIM fitting using physics-informed neural network with multimodal spatial prior
pairs.abstract: Purpose: To mitigate parameter degeneracy and improve robustness of IVIM fitting, a multimodal physics-informed neural network was developed to leverage anatomical information through the combined use of cross attention, selective spatial gating, and anatomy-weighted spatial prior. Methods: T1w and FLAIR anatomical images were co-registered to IVIM signal in native space and segmented by tissue type. The proposed Physics-Anchored Cross-attention Embedding network (PACE) encoded IVIM signals and their anatomical features in parallel branches, then integrated them via cross attention and spatial gating. An anatomy-weighted spatial prior further constrained signal reconstruction using anatomically similar neighboring voxels. PACE and its prior-guided variant were compared with two baseline deep neural networks (DNN and IVIM3C), least squares, non-negative least squares, and maximum a posteriori fitting models. All models were evaluated on signal and parameter reconstruction accuracy and lesion contrast fidelity using data generated from subjects drawn from the University of Rochester COVID cohort. Results: PACE variants demonstrated lower RMSE for all IVIM parameters except for Dmv. The anatomy-weighted spatial prior further reduced RMSE across all five parameters relative to the default PACE, with modest reductions in lesion contrast accuracy for fmv and fint. For in-vivo evaluation, PACE with spatial prior also showed the best signal reconstruction across all noise levels while maintaining good to excellent ICC. Conclusion: Multimodal anatomical information improved IVIM fitting accuracy and robustness, with selective spatial integration via cross attention, gating, and anatomy-weighted spatial prior. Keywords: intravoxel incoherent motion, physics-informed deep learning, diffusion MRI, multimodality fusion, attention mechanism
pairs.old: The paper addresses instability and parameter degeneracy in intravoxel incoherent motion fitting by incorporating anatomical MRI into a neural network designed to reconstruct diffusion signals and estimate model parameters. The method uses parallel branches for IVIM and anatomical inputs, then combines them with cross attention, selective spatial gating, and an anatomy-weighted spatial prior that borrows information from similar neighboring voxels. Compared with least-squares, Bayesian, and other deep learning baselines, the proposed models reduced parameter RMSE and improved signal reconstruction robustness across noise levels, with the spatial prior giving the strongest overall gains.
pairs.new:
Cross-attention plus anatomy-weighted spatial priors cut IVIM parameter RMSE and improved signal reconstruction robustness.
PACE encodes IVIM signals alongside co-registered T1w and FLAIR anatomy, then fuses them with cross attention, selective spatial gating, and an anatomy-weighted spatial prior. On data from the University of Rochester COVID cohort, PACE variants lowered RMSE for all IVIM parameters except Dmv, and the prior-guided version further reduced RMSE across all five parameters versus default PACE, with modest losses in lesion contrast accuracy for fmv and fint; in vivo, it gave the best signal reconstruction across all noise levels while maintaining good to excellent ICC.

pairs.title: Sequential Learning-Based Physics-Informed Neural Network Modeling for Parameter Estimation on a Power Converter
pairs.abstract: A staged physics-informed neural network (PINN) is proposed for identifying the inductance, capacitance and parasitic resistances of a DC buck converter from time-domain data. Gradients are released in the order of L to C to rL to rC, a sequence derived from sensitivity analysis. The five-stage schedule recovers L and C to within 5% and the series ESR to 10%, while a three-stage variant attains the same accuracy 11% faster. An 84 factorial sweep confirms that the trained PINN remains accurate for simultaneous 8% perturbations of all four components, achieving a waveform RMSE of 2.6 x 10-2 over 5 ms-an order-of-magnitude better than a simultaneous-training baseline.
pairs.old: The paper addresses parameter identification in a DC buck converter using a staged physics-informed neural network trained on time-domain measurements. It introduces a sequential gradient-release schedule, ordered by sensitivity analysis, to estimate inductance, capacitance, and parasitic resistances more effectively than simultaneous training. The method recovers key component values with low error and improves efficiency, while also showing robustness under simultaneous perturbations of all four parameters.
pairs.new:
Staged PINN recovers buck-converter L, C, and parasitics from time-domain data, with 11% faster training than a five-stage schedule.
A physics-informed neural network is trained in stages to identify a DC buck converter’s inductance, capacitance, and parasitic resistances, releasing gradients in the order L, C, rL, then rC based on sensitivity analysis. The five-stage schedule estimates L and C within 5% and the series ESR within 10%; a three-stage variant reaches the same accuracy 11% faster, and an 84-factorial sweep shows robustness to simultaneous 8% perturbations of all four components with waveform RMSE 2.6 x 10-2 over 5 ms, about an order of magnitude better than simultaneous training.

pairs.title: Hard-Constrained Physics--Informed Neural Network with Adaptive Regional Residual Balancing for the Generalized Falkner--Skan Problem
pairs.abstract: We present a physics--informed neural solver for the generalized Falkner--Skan boundary-value problem that combines an exact boundary--admissible trial representation with adaptive regional residual balancing (ARRB). The three prescribed boundary conditions are embedded analytically, eliminating boundary-condition penalty terms while allowing the finite--domain streamfunction value and wall shear to be determined by the governing equation. The residual is divided into wall, middle, and tail regions, and a physical global residual is reconstructed from regional mean-squared errors using region-length fractions. Safeguarded exponential--moving--average inverse--gradient coefficients adaptively balance the regional contributions during Adam optimization. A deterministic 800-point residual monitor is used for checkpoint selection, followed by two deterministic L--BFGS stages minimizing the physical global residual. The method is tested on the Blasius, favourable-pressure--gradient Falkner--Skan, and Pohlhausen cases. For \((β_0,β_1)=(0.75,0.50)\), the predicted wall shear is \(f''(0)=0.8997161394\), compared with the finite-domain reference \(0.8997168085\), giving an absolute error of \(6.691\times10^{-7}\). The residual MSE is \(6.357\times10^{-9}\), while the relative \(L_2\) errors in \(f'\) and \(f''\) are \(2.848\times10^{-6}\) and \(4.188\times10^{-5}\). A matched single--seed ablation shows that ARRB reduces residual MSE by 52.81\% relative to global--residual training and by 50.24\% relative to equal-regional weighting. Wall--shear errors are reduced by 77.30\% and 72.37\%, respectively. These results support ARRB as an accuracy-oriented residual-conditioning strategy, while multi--seed experiments remain necessary to quantify optimization variability.
pairs.old: The paper addresses a boundary-value fluid mechanics problem by building a neural solver that enforces the boundary conditions exactly through an analytic trial form. It then splits the governing-equation residual into wall, middle, and tail regions and adaptively reweights those regional losses during training, followed by deterministic L-BFGS refinement. On benchmark Falkner–Skan cases, the method achieves very small residuals and highly accurate wall-shear predictions, with the reported adaptive balancing improving both residual error and shear accuracy over simpler weighting schemes.
pairs.new:
Exact boundary embedding plus adaptive regional residual balancing cuts Falkner–Skan wall-shear error to 6.691×10^-7.
A physics-informed neural solver for the generalized Falkner–Skan boundary-value problem embeds all three boundary conditions analytically, then splits the residual into wall, middle, and tail regions and balances them with safeguarded exponential-moving-average inverse-gradient weights during Adam, followed by two deterministic L-BFGS stages. On the b2_0,b2_1)=(0.75,0.50) case, it predicts f''(0)=0.8997161394 versus the finite-domain reference 0.8997168085, with absolute error 6.691×10^-7, residual MSE 6.357×10^-9, and relative L2 errors of 2.848×10^-6 for f' and 4.188×10^-5 for f''; a matched single-seed ablation reports 52.81% lower residual MSE than global-residual training and 50.24% lower than equal-regional weighting, with wall-shear errors reduced by 77.30% and 72.37%.

pairs.title: An Empirical Study of Counterfactual Self-Explanations in LLMs
pairs.abstract: Large language models can easily generate explanations for their own outputs, but such self-explanations are not necessarily faithful to the model's behavior. We study this issue through counterfactual self-explanations, where a model minimally edits an input so that its own prediction changes. Across sentiment analysis and natural language inference, we evaluate ten instruction-tuned models from the LLaMA-3 and Qwen-2.5 families, measuring faithfulness, minimality, and alignment with human-annotated rationales. Our results show that model scale is the strongest determinant of explanation quality: larger models are substantially more likely to generate counterfactuals that flip their own predictions and target decision-relevant evidence. In contrast, the rationale-guided condition produces edit-minimal counterfactuals that are also more human-aligned. However, it does not consistently improve faithfulness. Overall, counterfactual self-explanations can provide useful behavioral evidence about model decisions, but their reliability depends strongly on model capacity and should be empirically validated rather than assumed.
pairs.old: This paper examines whether large language models can produce faithful self-explanations by generating minimal counterfactual edits that change their own predictions. The authors test ten instruction-tuned models from the LLaMA-3 and Qwen-2.5 families on sentiment analysis and natural language inference, evaluating faithfulness, minimality, and agreement with human rationales. They find that larger models produce better counterfactual explanations and are more likely to target decision-relevant evidence, while rationale-guided prompting yields more minimal and human-aligned edits. However, the rationale-guided setup does not reliably improve faithfulness, so the study concludes that such explanations should be empirically validated rather than assumed trustworthy.
pairs.new:
Counterfactual self-explanations become more faithful with scale, but rationale guidance mainly improves minimality and human alignment.
Evaluates counterfactual self-explanations on sentiment analysis and natural language inference across ten instruction-tuned LLaMA-3 and Qwen-2.5 models, measuring faithfulness, minimality, and alignment with human rationales. Larger models were substantially more likely to produce counterfactuals that flipped their own predictions and focused on decision-relevant evidence; rationale-guided edits were more minimal and more human-aligned, but did not consistently improve faithfulness.

pairs.title: Solving Linear Systems in $\widetilde{O}(mn \log \fracκε)$ Bit Operations
pairs.abstract: We give a deterministic algorithm that solves a nonsingular linear system $Ax=b$, where $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ has $m$ nonzero entries and condition number $κ$, to any relative residual tolerance $0<ε\le1/2$ using $\widetilde{O(}mn\log(κ/ε))$ bit operations for inputs with logarithmically many bits per entry. For sparse, polynomially conditioned systems with $m=\widetilde{O}(n)$, this gives an $\widetilde{O}(n^2)$ algorithm for any inverse-polynomial accuracy, improving on the algorithm of Peng and Vempala, as sharpened by Nie, whose running time in this regime is approximately $O(n^{2.2707})$ with the best current matrix multiplication exponent, and largely closing a gap between the idealized performance of the conjugate gradient method in exact arithmetic and the running time achievable with finite-precision computation that has persisted for over 70 years. The algorithm is surprisingly simple. For integer inputs, we apply Dixon's lifting algorithm to the perturbed system $(A+I/R)x=b$ for a suitable integer $R$. After scaling, the matrix of this system is $RA+I\equiv I\pmod R$, so its modular inverse is trivial, and each lifting step needs only a sparse matrix-vector product with $A$ on $O(\log R)$-bit numbers. Fast rational reconstruction then recovers the exact solution of the perturbed system, which is an $ε$-accurate solution of the original one. Normalization and rounding extend the result to fixed-point and floating-point inputs, with floating-point outputs represented using short integer significands and a common encoded exponent. A computable certificate removes the need for prior knowledge of $κ$.
pairs.old: The paper studies deterministic algorithms for solving nonsingular linear systems with sparse matrices under finite-precision input models, targeting both approximate and exact computation. It combines Dixon-style lifting on a perturbed system with modular inversion, sparse matrix-vector products, and rational reconstruction to obtain an accurate solution efficiently. The main result is a bit-complexity bound of ˜O(mn log(κ/ε)) and, for sparse well-conditioned systems, an ˜O(n^2) algorithm for inverse-polynomial accuracy. It also provides a computable certificate that avoids requiring prior knowledge of the condition number.
pairs.new:
Deterministic sparse linear solves in ~mn log(κ/ε) bit operations, with an O(n^2) regime for m=~O(n).
Gives a deterministic algorithm for nonsingular Ax=b with m nonzeros and condition number κ, reaching relative residual tolerance ε in ~O(mn log(κ/ε)) bit operations for inputs with logarithmically many bits per entry. For sparse, polynomially conditioned systems with m=~O(n), this becomes an ~O(n^2) algorithm for inverse-polynomial accuracy; the method perturbs to A+I/R, uses Dixon lifting on RA+I ≡ I mod R, then applies rational reconstruction, with normalization and rounding extending it to fixed-point and floating-point inputs and a computable certificate removing the need to know κ in advance.

pairs.title: Discovery of Singularities in Partial Differential Equations Using Adaptive Numerical Discretizations
pairs.abstract: We compute self-similar singularity profiles of partial differential equations (PDEs) using adaptive numerical discretizations based on optimizing a discrete loss (ODIL). The fields are represented in overlapping local Chebyshev patches joined with a mapped asymptotic patch. After factoring out the leading power laws of solution ansatzes, their limiting amplitudes at infinity are determined by the optimization, eliminating domain truncation and prescribed far-field conditions. Adaptive refinement is guided by Chebyshev-coefficient decay, and the nonlinear least-squares problem is solved using automatically differentiated Gauss--Newton iterations with Levenberg--Marquardt damping. The method achieves O(10^{-14})-level accuracy for Burgers profiles, residuals of O(10^{-14}) to O(10^{-10}) for the generalized De Gregorio family, and of O(10^{-8}) in a local region for the two-dimensional Boussinesq equations. These results demonstrate that ODIL can identify singularity profiles for PDEs with high accuracy using adaptive numerical methods, complementing ongoing efforts that rely on artificial intelligence.
pairs.old: The paper addresses how to compute self-similar singularity profiles of partial differential equations with high accuracy using adaptive numerical discretizations. It represents the solution on overlapping Chebyshev patches plus a mapped asymptotic patch, then optimizes a discrete loss to determine both the profile and the far-field amplitudes without truncating the domain. Refinement is driven by Chebyshev-coefficient decay, and the resulting nonlinear least-squares problem is solved with automatically differentiated Gauss-Newton iterations and Levenberg-Marquardt damping. The method reports near machine-precision accuracy for Burgers profiles and very small residuals for the generalized De Gregorio family and the two-dimensional Boussinesq equations.
pairs.new:
ODIL recovers self-similar singularity profiles with 10^-14 accuracy and no prescribed far-field conditions.
Fields are represented in overlapping local Chebyshev patches plus a mapped asymptotic patch, and the leading power laws are factored out so the far-field amplitudes are determined by optimization rather than imposed boundary conditions. Using adaptive refinement from Chebyshev-coefficient decay and autodifferentiated Gauss-Newton with Levenberg-Marquardt damping, the method reaches O(10^-14) accuracy for Burgers profiles, residuals of O(10^-14) to O(10^-10) for the generalized De Gregorio family, and O(10^-8) in a local region for the 2D Boussinesq equations.

pairs.title: Higher-Order QMC $hp$-FEM UQ for Singular Perturbation: Reaction-Diffusion with Gevrey-Parametric Reaction Coefficient
pairs.abstract: We analyze the combined discretization of singularly perturbed reaction-diffusion problems with perturbation parameter $\varepsilon\in (0,1]$ and with parametric, Gevrey-regular reaction term, by $hp$-Galerkin FE methods and by higher-order polynomial lattice rules. We establish $\varepsilon$-robust algebraic convergence rates for the combined QMC $hp$-FEM approximation that are not subject to the curse of dimensionality (CoD) in the parametric reaction coefficient, and only limited by the sparsity and the $\mathfrak{s}_{y}$-Gevrey regularity of the reaction coefficient expansion. On the interval $(-1,1)$, we establish an $\varepsilon$-robust, root-exponential convergence rate $\exp(-σ\, p_{\mathrm{FE}}^{1/\mathfrak{s}_{x}})$ for $hp$-Galerkin FEM for reaction-diffusion problems under $\mathfrak{s}_{x}$-Gevrey regularity assumptions on the reaction coefficient and the source term, a result that can be of independent interest. Numerical experiments are consistent with the theoretical bounds.
pairs.old: The paper studies singularly perturbed reaction-diffusion equations with a parametric reaction coefficient and analyzes a combined discretization using hp-Galerkin finite elements and higher-order polynomial lattice rules. It proves ε-robust algebraic convergence for the full approximation, with rates governed by the sparsity and Gevrey regularity of the coefficient expansion rather than by the parameter dimension. In one-dimensional settings, it also establishes a root-exponential convergence rate for the hp-FEM discretization under Gevrey regularity assumptions on the coefficient and source term. Numerical experiments are reported to match the theoretical convergence behavior.
pairs.new:
Combines hp-FEM and higher-order QMC with ε-robust algebraic convergence, avoiding dimension curse in Gevrey-parametric reaction-diffusion.
Analyzes singularly perturbed reaction-diffusion problems with ε in (0,1] and a Gevrey-regular parametric reaction term using hp-Galerkin FEM plus higher-order polynomial lattice rules. Proves ε-robust algebraic convergence for the combined QMC hp-FEM approximation, limited only by sparsity and the s_y-Gevrey regularity of the coefficient expansion, and on (-1,1) proves an ε-robust root-exponential rate exp(-σ p_FE^{1/s_x}) for hp-FEM under s_x-Gevrey assumptions on the coefficient and source term; numerics match the theory.

pairs.title: From Local Atomic Motifs to Thermodynamic State: An Interpretable Physics-Informed Framework for Cu-Zr Metallic Glasses
pairs.abstract: Machine-learning models that relate local atomic structure to the thermodynamic state of metallic glasses typically assess physical consistency after training rather than enforcing it during learning. Here, we develop a multi-task physics-informed neural network (PINN) that predicts temperature directly from Voronoi-motif population histograms while incorporating autograd-derived gradient constraints representing physically motivated relationships between structural motifs, quench rate, and temperature. The model simultaneously classifies each configuration as liquid, supercooled/transition, or glass through an auxiliary classification head. The classification task achieves 96.6% test accuracy with a macro-F1 score of 0.95, while the regression head yields a mean absolute error of 23.4 K on a trajectory-disjoint held-out test set. Five-fold trajectory-grouped cross-validation, deep-ensemble predictions, and Monte Carlo dropout are used to assess model robustness and predictive uncertainty. Sensitivity analyses demonstrate that physics constraints can be incorporated over a broad range of loss weights without compromising predictive accuracy, while substantially improving compliance with the prescribed physical trends. Benchmarking against conventional machine-learning regressors further demonstrates competitive predictive performance. SHAP analysis across the cross-validation ensemble identifies the coupled near-icosahedral motif family, particularly the full icosahedral motif and its single-atom-perturbed counterpart, as the dominant structural fingerprints of the glassy state. These results demonstrate that physically motivated constraints can be embedded directly into motif-based structure-property models, providing a pathway from post-hoc interpretability toward physically constrained machine learning for metallic glasses.
pairs.old: The paper develops a multi-task neural network for predicting the thermodynamic state of Cu-Zr metallic glasses from local structural motif histograms, with explicit gradient-based constraints built into training. It combines a temperature regression head with a phase-classification head and evaluates robustness using grouped cross-validation, deep ensembles, and Monte Carlo dropout. The model achieves strong classification performance and low temperature error, while the added physical constraints improve adherence to expected structural trends without hurting accuracy.
pairs.new:
A PINN predicts Cu-Zr temperature from Voronoi motifs with 23.4 K MAE and 96.6% phase classification accuracy.
A multi-task physics-informed neural network maps Voronoi-motif population histograms to temperature while enforcing autograd-based gradient constraints tied to motif, quench-rate, and temperature relationships. On a trajectory-disjoint test set, the regression head reaches 23.4 K mean absolute error and the auxiliary liquid/supercooled-glass classifier reaches 96.6% accuracy with macro-F1 0.95; five-fold trajectory-grouped cross-validation, deep ensembles, and Monte Carlo dropout are used for robustness and uncertainty, and SHAP points to the coupled near-icosahedral motif family as the main glassy-state fingerprint.

pairs.title: A Local Stabilized Isogeometric Formulation with Discontinuous Pressure for Mesh-Conforming and Immersed Analysis of Nearly Incompressible Elasticity
pairs.abstract: Nearly incompressible materials arise in soft tissues, elastomers, gels, and other soft solids. Yet, numerical modeling remains challenging because displacement-based formulations can exhibit volumetric locking near incompressibility. Mixed displacement-pressure formulations address this difficulty but require compatible approximation spaces satisfying the inf-sup condition. In mixed formulations, discontinuous pressure spaces are attractive since pressure degrees of freedom can be condensed locally. In high-order isogeometric analysis, however, their Galerkin stability requires pressure-grid coarsening that increases with polynomial degree. Here, we develop a variational multiscale (VMS) stabilized mixed isogeometric formulation that retains this locality while substantially relaxing the restriction. The key observation is that VMS stabilization controls nonconstant elementwise pressure modes and is unconditionally stable with respect to its parameter, provided the elementwise constant pressure component satisfies the inf-sup condition. Consequently, for maximally continuous displacement splines, a pressure grid coarsened by a factor of two satisfies the constant-mode inf-sup criterion independently of polynomial degree. Local condensation then yields a displacement-only system, facilitating use in existing displacement solvers. The formulation is further extended to immersed isogeometric analysis with extended B-splines, pressure-cell aggregation, subdivision-based cut-cell quadrature, and weak enforcement of essential boundary conditions. Discrete inf-sup studies and convergence analyses in the Kirsch and Cook's membrane benchmarks demonstrate stability and show that the immersed treatment preserves mixed stability properties. The proposed framework therefore provides a local, high-order, and robust approach for nearly incompressible problems in mesh-conforming and immersed settings.
pairs.old: The paper addresses numerical difficulties in nearly incompressible elasticity, where standard displacement methods can lock and mixed displacement-pressure methods can be unstable unless the approximation spaces are carefully chosen. It proposes a variational multiscale stabilized mixed isogeometric formulation with discontinuous pressure that preserves local condensation while relaxing the usual pressure-grid coarsening requirements. The method is extended to immersed isogeometric analysis with cut-cell quadrature and weak boundary enforcement. Benchmarks and inf-sup studies show stable behavior and good convergence, including in mesh-conforming and immersed settings.
pairs.new:
VMS stabilization makes discontinuous-pressure isogeometric mixed methods locally condensable with only 2x pressure coarsening, independent of polynomial degree.
Develops a variational multiscale stabilized mixed isogeometric formulation for nearly incompressible elasticity that keeps discontinuous pressure local and allows static condensation to a displacement-only system. For maximally continuous displacement splines, a pressure grid coarsened by a factor of two satisfies the constant-mode inf-sup condition regardless of polynomial degree, and the immersed extension with extended B-splines, pressure-cell aggregation, cut-cell quadrature, and weak boundary enforcement passes discrete inf-sup and convergence tests on Kirsch and Cook's membrane benchmarks.

pairs.title: A Fast and Stable Square-Root-Free Unitary Core-Chasing Algorithm
pairs.abstract: Symmetric and unitary matrices are among the most important classes of structured matrices admitting efficient and stable eigenvalue algorithms. Notable examples include structure-preserving variants of the QR algorithm and their square-root-free counterparts. For unitary matrices, these algorithms were historically derived from recurrence relations for orthogonal polynomials on the unit circle. A matrix-based derivation using core chasing was later given in [3]; this family of algorithms is backward stable, but the underlying symmetries needed to cast out the square roots were not identified, and the question of structured backward stability was left open. In this paper we present a matrix-based derivation of the symmetric unitary core-chasing algorithm and use it to obtain a square-root-free variant. We give a matrix-based proof of backward stability and show that strict structured backward stability is impossible in general. Open-source Fortran code and numerical experiments demonstrate that the combination of exploiting the symmetry and removing the square roots reduces computation time without degrading accuracy.
pairs.old: The paper studies fast eigenvalue algorithms for symmetric unitary matrices, focusing on a structure-preserving core-chasing method and a square-root-free variant. It develops a matrix-based derivation, proves backward stability, and analyzes why strict structured backward stability cannot generally be achieved. The authors also provide open-source Fortran code and numerical experiments showing that removing square roots and exploiting symmetry reduces runtime without harming accuracy.
pairs.new:
Square-root-free unitary core chasing cuts runtime while preserving backward stability, with a matrix-based derivation and proof.
Derives a matrix-based symmetric unitary core-chasing algorithm and a square-root-free variant, then proves backward stability for the method. It also shows strict structured backward stability is impossible in general, and Fortran experiments indicate that exploiting symmetry and removing square roots reduces computation time without degrading accuracy.

pairs.title: Regional accuracy of physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) for recirculation in a deep lid-driven cavity
pairs.abstract: Deep lid-driven cavities contain strong motion beneath the lid and much weaker recirculation at depth, so agreement in bulk velocity is an incomplete assessment of a computed flow. We examine data-free physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) for steady, two-dimensional incompressible flow in a cavity of depth-to-width ratio five at Reynolds numbers 100, 250, 500 and 1000. An established hard-constrained streamfunction formulation is combined with prescribed regional collocation, transferred initialization, and selected residual-scaling and envelope variants. Independent spectral/$hp$ calculations with the same Gaussian-regularized lid provide the reference fields. For a cavity of depth-to-width ratio $D/W=5$ at Reynolds numbers $\mathrm{Re}=100$, 250, 500, and 1000, evaluation on a common $121\times605$ grid gives interior relative velocity discrepancies of 5.130\%--7.850\%. Over the same cases, floor-region relative velocity discrepancies remain below 5\%, with absolute RMS discrepancies ranging from $1.255\times10^{-10}U$ to $2.332\times10^{-9}U$, where $U$ is the lid-velocity scale. In a separate $161\times801$ assessment at $\Rey=1000$, the refined workflow lowers interior velocity discrepancy from 5.624\% to 2.658\% and gauge-aligned pressure RMS discrepancy from $2.793\times10^{-3}$ to $1.167\times10^{-3}ρU^2$. The improvements compare accumulated training workflows and do not isolate regional sampling. Configuration rankings depend on both region and observable. These finite-budget comparisons establish where the retained workflows agree with the reference and where rotational-field discrepancies remain substantial.
pairs.old: This paper studies data-free physics-informed neural networks for steady incompressible flow in a deep lid-driven cavity, using a hard-constrained streamfunction formulation and several training refinements such as regional collocation, transferred initialization, residual scaling, and envelope variants. The authors compare PINN predictions against high-order spectral/hp reference solutions across multiple Reynolds numbers and grid evaluations, with particular attention to how errors vary between the interior and the near-floor recirculation region. They report interior velocity discrepancies of about 5.1%–7.9%, floor-region discrepancies below 5%, and further improvements in a refined workflow at Re=1000 that reduce both velocity and pressure errors. The results show that performance depends strongly on region and observable, highlighting where the trained models match the reference well and where significant discrepancies remain.
pairs.new:
Regional sampling and transferred initialization cut Re=1000 interior velocity error from 5.624% to 2.658% in a deep cavity.
Data-free PINNs were tested for steady 2D incompressible flow in a depth-to-width-5 lid-driven cavity at Re=100, 250, 500, and 1000, using hard-constrained streamfunction formulations plus regional collocation, transferred initialization, and residual-scaling/envelope variants. On a 121×605 grid, interior relative velocity discrepancies were 5.130%–7.850%, while floor-region discrepancies stayed below 5% with absolute RMS errors from 1.255×10^-10U to 2.332×10^-9U; on a separate 161×801 Re=1000 assessment, the refined workflow reduced interior velocity discrepancy from 5.624% to 2.658% and gauge-aligned pressure RMS discrepancy from 2.793×10^-3 to 1.167×10^-3 ρU^2.

pairs.title: Randomly shifted lattice rules for SDEs with constant diffusion: error bounds uniform in time discretization and dimension
pairs.abstract: We study randomly shifted rank-1 lattice rules for computing $\mathbb{E}[g(\mathbf{X}_T)]$, where $\mathbf{X}_T$ is the terminal state of a stochastic differential equation (SDE) with constant diffusion matrix. Discretizing the SDE by the Euler--Maruyama scheme with $m$ uniform time steps turns the expectation into an integral whose dimension grows with $m$ and whose integrand has a nested composition structure; both complicate the lattice rule error analysis. We generate the Brownian path by the Brownian bridge construction and handle the nested structure using the multivariate Faà di Bruno formula and a rooted-tree expansion. Under suitable regularity and growth conditions, we prove that an $N$-point randomly shifted lattice rule with a uniformly random generating vector achieves a mean absolute sampling error of $O(N^{-1+\varepsilon})$ for every $\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)$ and every prime $N$, with the implied constant independent of $m$. To improve stability and control higher error moments, the median lattice estimator is used. The estimator takes the median of $R=2k-1$ independent lattice estimates and achieves an $L^q$ error of $O(N^{-1+\varepsilon})$ for every $1\le q<k/(1-\varepsilon)$. We further establish error bounds independent of both the state dimension and the Brownian path dimension under an additional summability condition on the columns of the diffusion matrix. Numerical experiments show that median lattice estimators converge faster than Monte Carlo estimators and remain stable as the number of time steps $m$ grows. For models satisfying the additional summability condition, stability is also observed as the state and Brownian path dimensions increase.
pairs.old: The paper analyzes randomized lattice rules for estimating expectations of SDE terminal states after Euler–Maruyama discretization, with the main challenge being that the resulting integrand has growing dimension and nested composition structure. It develops a Brownian bridge construction together with multivariate Faà di Bruno and rooted-tree expansions to derive dimension- and time-discretization-uniform error bounds. The main result is an $O(N^{-1+\varepsilon})$ mean absolute error for randomly shifted rank-1 lattice rules, with constants independent of the number of time steps, and under an extra summability condition also independent of the state and Brownian path dimensions. Numerical experiments confirm faster convergence and improved stability over Monte Carlo as the discretization and dimensions increase.
pairs.new:
Randomly shifted lattice rules get O(N^{-1+ε}) SDE terminal-value error uniformly in time discretization, with median stabilization.
For Euler--Maruyama discretizations with m uniform time steps, the paper analyzes rank-1 lattice rules after Brownian bridge construction and proves mean absolute sampling error O(N^{-1+ε}) for every ε in (0,1/2) and every prime N, with constants independent of m. Using the median of R=2k-1 independent lattice estimates gives L^q error O(N^{-1+ε}) for every 1≤q<k/(1-ε), and under an added summability condition on diffusion columns the bounds are also independent of state and Brownian path dimension; experiments report faster convergence than Monte Carlo and stability as m grows, with dimension stability in the summable case.

pairs.title: Randomized Symplectic Model Reduction: One-Pass Basis Construction and Sketched Hamiltonian Assembly
pairs.abstract: Symplectic model order reduction of Hamiltonian systems yields reduced dynamics that conserve the reduced Hamiltonian along exact trajectories, avoiding the artificial energy drift that can arise from conventional projection methods. For large-scale spatial discretizations, however, basis construction and reduced-operator assembly can involve substantial offline costs. Randomized numerical linear algebra can reduce these costs through low-dimensional sketches while supporting streaming and parallel implementations. We develop randomized techniques for two parts of the offline stage while preserving the Hamiltonian structure of the reduced dynamics. First, we introduce the one-pass sketched randomized cSVD (Ops-rcSVD), a one-pass randomized variant of the complex-SVD algorithm. Combining randomized range finding with an independent left sketch, Ops-rcSVD constructs an ortho-symplectic reduced basis from a single pass over the snapshot ensemble. Second, for quadratic Hamiltonian systems, we introduce a randomized reduced-Hamiltonian assembly based on sketching the reduced basis and operator actions, yielding a reduced Hamiltonian system by construction. We derive bounds for the snapshot projection error, uniform-in-parameter perturbation bounds for the sketched reduced Hamiltonian, and an energy-norm estimate for the difference between reduced and sketched reduced trajectories. Experiments on large-scale systems show that Ops-rcSVD attains projection accuracy comparable to deterministic and two-pass randomized constructions while reducing basis-construction time. They further demonstrate accurate sketched reduced-Hamiltonian assembly when storing the complete snapshot ensemble is no longer feasible.
pairs.old: The paper develops randomized numerical linear algebra methods for constructing symplectic reduced bases and assembling reduced Hamiltonians for large-scale Hamiltonian systems. Its main technical contributions are a one-pass sketched randomized cSVD algorithm and a sketched reduced-operator assembly procedure that preserve the Hamiltonian structure by construction. The authors prove error and perturbation bounds for the snapshot projection, the sketched reduced Hamiltonian, and the resulting trajectories. Experiments indicate that the proposed methods achieve accuracy comparable to deterministic and two-pass randomized approaches while lowering offline computational cost and memory requirements.
pairs.new:
One-pass symplectic basis construction and sketched Hamiltonian assembly cut offline costs without breaking reduced Hamiltonian structure.
Introduces Ops-rcSVD, a one-pass randomized variant of complex-SVD that combines randomized range finding with an independent left sketch to build an ortho-symplectic reduced basis from a single snapshot pass. For quadratic Hamiltonian systems, it also sketches the reduced basis and operator actions to assemble a reduced Hamiltonian by construction, with bounds for snapshot projection error, uniform-in-parameter perturbation of the sketched reduced Hamiltonian, and an energy-norm estimate for reduced-versus-sketched trajectories; experiments report projection accuracy comparable to deterministic and two-pass randomized methods while reducing basis-construction time, and accurate assembly when the full snapshot ensemble cannot be stored.

pairs.title: SoftServe: A Scalable Quasi-Newton Method for Deep Learning
pairs.abstract: Quasi-Newton (QN) methods have long been among the most effective methods for large-scale unconstrained convex optimization. Two obstacles have limited their use in deep learning: non-convexity and enormous parameter sizes. We introduce SoftServe, a family of QN methods designed to overcome these obstacles without line searches or ad hoc curvature corrections. SoftServe derives positivedefinite curvature estimates from the variational objective of Berglund et al. (2025), even in the presence of negative curvature. We develop diagonal and Kroneckerfactored variants that preserve positive definiteness by construction and scale to massive neural networks. Finally, SoftServe relies on the stable coupled Newton-Schulz iteration for the required matrix operations, replacing costly matrix decompositions with GPU-friendly matrix multiplications. SoftServe excels on problems that are severely ill-conditioned, including tasks such as recurrent networks, deep autoencoders, physics-informed neural networks, and a 136M-parameter physics-informed diffusion model, often achieving lower losses than established baselines including Adam, Muon, and SOAP.
pairs.old: The paper addresses the difficulty of applying quasi-Newton optimization to large, nonconvex neural networks, where standard methods struggle with unstable curvature estimates and prohibitive matrix operations. It proposes SoftServe, a family of positive-definite quasi-Newton methods built from a variational objective, with diagonal and Kronecker-factored variants that are designed to scale efficiently using GPU-friendly Newton-Schulz iterations. The method is evaluated on severely ill-conditioned tasks including recurrent networks, deep autoencoders, and physics-informed neural networks, as well as a large physics-informed diffusion model. Results show that SoftServe often achieves lower losses than strong baselines such as Adam, Muon, and SOAP.
pairs.new:
Positive-definite quasi-Newton updates for deep nets, with diagonal and Kronecker-factored variants that scale to 136M parameters.
SoftServe is a family of quasi-Newton methods built from the variational objective of Berglund et al. (2025), designed to stay positive definite even with negative curvature and to avoid line searches or ad hoc curvature corrections. It uses the stable coupled Newton-Schulz iteration instead of matrix decompositions, and the paper reports lower losses than Adam, Muon, and SOAP on ill-conditioned tasks including recurrent networks, deep autoencoders, physics-informed neural networks, and a 136M-parameter physics-informed diffusion model.

pairs.title: asdex: Automatic Sparse Differentiation in JAX
pairs.abstract: Many tasks in scientific computing and machine learning require the Jacobian or Hessian matrix of a function. Automatic differentiation (AD) computes these derivatives to machine precision, but materializing a dense $m \times n$ Jacobian requires $n$ forward-mode or $m$ reverse-mode AD passes, one per column or row. For a large class of functions, each output depends on only a few inputs, making the derivative matrix sparse. Automatic sparse differentiation (ASD) exploits this structure in four steps: detection of the input-agnostic sparsity pattern, coloring of a graph to group columns or rows that can share an AD pass, compressed differentiation to compute a compressed derivative matrix with one AD pass per color, and finally decompression into the original sparsity pattern. The number of colors, and hence of AD passes, is often independent of the problem dimension: a banded Jacobian with $b$ contiguous bands, for instance, only ever requires $b$ colors, regardless of its size. asdex offers the first standalone ASD toolkit in the popular JAX ecosystem. With asdex.jacobian and asdex.hessian, it provides sparse drop-in replacements for jax.jacobian and jax.hessian.
pairs.old: The paper addresses the cost of computing Jacobians and Hessians when the derivative matrices are sparse, which is a common issue in scientific computing. It presents an automatic sparse differentiation framework that first detects sparsity structure, then uses graph coloring to reduce the number of automatic differentiation passes, followed by compressed differentiation and reconstruction. The implementation is provided as a standalone toolkit for JAX with drop-in Jacobian and Hessian routines. The headline result is that the number of derivative evaluations can depend on sparsity structure rather than full problem dimension, making large sparse derivatives much cheaper to compute.
pairs.new:
ASD in JAX cuts Jacobian/Hessian AD passes to the number of colors, often independent of problem size.
Introduces asdex, a standalone automatic sparse differentiation toolkit for JAX that detects input-agnostic sparsity, colors the dependency graph, computes a compressed derivative matrix with one AD pass per color, and then decompresses it. For a banded Jacobian with b contiguous bands, the abstract says only b colors are needed regardless of dimension, and asdex.jacobian and asdex.hessian are sparse drop-in replacements for jax.jacobian and jax.hessian.

pairs.title: An arbitrarily high-order accurate and locally energy/entropy-stable space-time method for a class of nonlinear wave systems
pairs.abstract: We present a new class of structure-preserving, arbitrarily high-order accurate space-time schemes using unstructured simplicial meshes in space for a class of nonlinear acoustic wave propagation systems, in which the nonlinearity is encoded in the constitutive relations between the state and dual variables, while the differential operators retain the standard first-order acoustic wave structure. At the fully discrete level, the schemes satisfy the following properties: I) local conservation of the state variables; II) a local energy/entropy balance on each space-time element, with a consistent, single-valued numerical energy/entropy flux and nonnegative local energy/entropy dissipation, and exact energy conservation when the stabilization terms are omitted; III) weak preservation of the curl involution of the velocity field, even in the presence of discontinuities and with the shock-capturing terms activated. The key ingredients of the new schemes are: i) a discontinuous Galerkin (DG) discretization in space, in which the dual variables are computed as the L2 projections onto the DG space of the energy derivatives with respect to the conserved variables; ii) numerical fluxes and a bubble-weighted, element-local viscous regularization expressed in terms of the dual variables; iii) a continuous-discontinuous Petrov-Galerkin method in time. Properties I)-III) are first proved mathematically and are then verified by suitable numerical tests.
pairs.old: The paper develops a new family of arbitrarily high-order space-time discretizations for nonlinear acoustic wave systems on unstructured simplicial meshes. It combines discontinuous Galerkin methods in space with a continuous-discontinuous Petrov-Galerkin treatment in time, along with fluxes and local viscous regularization written in terms of dual variables. The authors prove that the fully discrete schemes conserve the state locally, satisfy a local energy/entropy balance with nonnegative dissipation, and preserve the curl involution weakly even with shocks. These properties are then confirmed with numerical experiments.
pairs.new:
Space-time DG schemes that prove local conservation, local energy/entropy balance, and curl preservation for nonlinear acoustic waves.
Introduces arbitrarily high-order space-time schemes on unstructured simplicial meshes for nonlinear acoustic wave systems, with nonlinearity placed in constitutive relations while the differential operators stay first-order. At the fully discrete level, the method is proved to give local conservation of the state variables, a local energy/entropy balance with single-valued flux and nonnegative dissipation, exact energy conservation without stabilization, and weak preservation of the velocity curl involution; these properties are then checked in numerical tests.

pairs.title: Sensitivity-Guided Parameter Estimation of Bubbly Liquid via a Nonlinear Wave Equation and Physics-InformedNeuralNetworks
pairs.abstract: Interactions between ultrasound and microbubbles underlie a range of biomedical and industrial applications, yet predicting how the physical parameters of the medium and bubbles govern nonlinear wave propagation remains difficult. This study proposes a parameter estimation framework that combines a Korteweg-de Vries-Burgers (KdVB) equation, describing weakly nonlinear wave propagation in a bubbly liquid, with a physics-informed neural network (PINN). The contributions are threefold. First, the PINN reproduces the reference solution of the governing equation in the forward problem, with a near-zero prediction error at the initial time that confirms the initial condition is enforced exactly as intended. Second, prior to inverse estimation, a sensitivity analysis is introduced that quantifies, at both the coefficient and solution levels, how each of eight physical parameters influences the KdVB equation, allowing the expected difficulty of estimating each parameter to be assessed in advance. Third, based on this assessment, single-parameter inverse estimation is performed for seven of the eight parameters using the PINN. Liquid viscosity, bubble initial radius, liquid density, sound speed, and liquid pressure are estimated with errors of 0.8-2.1%, the polytropic exponent converges only partially, and the surface tension coefficient cannot be estimated at all, consistent with the sensitivity analysis. These results establish a general framework for identifying and estimating the physical parameters governing nonlinear wave propagation in bubbly liquids from observed waveform data.
pairs.old: The paper develops a physics-informed neural network framework for a nonlinear wave equation governing weakly nonlinear propagation in bubbly liquids, with the network used both to solve the forward problem and to estimate unknown physical parameters from waveform data. A sensitivity analysis is added to assess how strongly each of eight coefficients affects the equation and its solution, guiding which parameters are likely identifiable. In inverse experiments, seven single-parameter estimates are attempted, with several parameters recovered to within 0.8–2.1% error, while one parameter converges only partially and another cannot be estimated. The results show that parameter identifiability varies substantially across coefficients and that the sensitivity study aligns with the estimation outcomes.
pairs.new:
Sensitivity analysis predicts which bubbly-liquid parameters a PINN can recover before inverse estimation starts.
Combines a Korteweg-de Vries-Burgers model for weakly nonlinear wave propagation in bubbly liquid with a physics-informed neural network, first matching the forward solution with near-zero error at the initial time. Using sensitivity analysis on eight physical parameters, it then estimates seven one at a time: viscosity, initial bubble radius, density, sound speed, and liquid pressure are recovered with 0.8-2.1% error, the polytropic exponent converges only partially, and surface tension cannot be estimated.

pairs.title: CEENs: Causality-enforced evolutional networks for solving time-dependent partial differential equations
pairs.abstract: Despite the growing popularity of physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), their applicability in the long-time integration of partial differential equations (PDEs) remains constrained. We argue that this problem stems from the lack of consideration of temporal causality in the original PINN formulation, resulting in a bias towards satisfying governing equations at later times before learning the initial condition and hence leading to erroneous solutions. To this end, we propose a novel method that seamlessly integrates temporal causality into the training process. Drawing inspiration from classical numerical methods where the temporal causality is reflected, we divide the time domain into nonoverlapping subintervals, assign a unique neural network to each subinterval, and construct a loss function founded on the integral form of PDEs within these subintervals. The proposed networks undergo sequential training, beginning with the initial time step. Our method demonstrates significant improvement in accuracy for long-time simulations of various PDE problems where the original PINN method fails while it requires less computational cost and memory compared to the PINN method. A parallelization algorithm is provided to further enhance the computational efficiency, showing a significant speedup for solving time-dependent PDEs.
pairs.old: The paper addresses a key limitation in physics-informed neural networks for long-time simulation of time-dependent partial differential equations: training can drift toward later times before the initial condition is properly learned. It proposes causality-enforced evolutional networks that split the time domain into nonoverlapping subintervals, use a separate neural network on each interval, and train them sequentially from the initial time onward with a loss based on the integral form of the PDE. The method improves accuracy on several PDE benchmarks where standard PINN training fails, while also reducing computational cost and memory use. A parallelization scheme is included to further speed up training and inference for time-dependent problems.
pairs.new:
Sequential subinterval training enforces temporal causality in PINNs, improving long-time PDE solves while cutting cost and memory.
Divides the time domain into nonoverlapping subintervals, assigns one neural network per subinterval, and trains them sequentially from the initial time using a loss built from the integral form of the PDE on each subinterval. The method reports significantly better accuracy on long-time simulations of various PDE problems where the original PINN fails, with lower computational cost and memory, and a parallelization algorithm that gives a significant speedup.

pairs.title: Low Residuals, Wrong Value: Learning the Viscosity Solution of Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs Equations with PINNs
pairs.abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) and other residual-trained solvers judge a candidate solution by the size of its sampled PDE residual. For first-order Hamilton-Jacobi equations this is not sufficient: the same equation and boundary data admit Lipschitz almost-everywhere solutions that differ from the viscosity solution by $O(1)$ while violating the equation only on sets of measure zero. We study whether residual minimization selects such solutions in a fixed-horizon pursuit-evasion game whose Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs value function is known in closed form on the circle $S^1$ and on the flat tori $\mathbb{T}^{2}$ and $\mathbb{T}^{4}$. We train four neural parameterizations with ten seeds on each geometry, 120 runs in total. A standard network with periodic Fourier features converges to folded almost-everywhere solutions in all 30 runs: small residuals and the expected capture-layer gradient, yet values that are wrong over most of the domain. A network with periodicity imposed through the loss recovers the viscosity solution in one and two dimensions but becomes unreliable in four. Two parameterizations that receive the geodesic distance do substantially better: a single network fed the wrapped displacement and its distance recovers the viscosity solution in all 30 runs, while a minimum over periodic image charts succeeds in 27 of 30 and introduces a wrong-image failure mode. Finally, for the convex Hamiltonian considered here, we use the semiconcavity of the viscosity solution to build a mesh-free finite-difference test that needs only forward network evaluations; it detects the folded solutions and the harmful min-of-charts failures without access to the exact value function. A small sampled residual thus does not by itself validate a learned Hamilton-Jacobi solution; the parameterization and independent structural diagnostics can be essential for selecting the viscosity solution.
pairs.old: This paper studies a failure mode of residual-trained neural solvers for first-order Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equations, showing that small sampled PDE residuals can correspond to solutions that are qualitatively wrong. The authors compare several neural parameterizations on a pursuit-evasion game with known closed-form value functions on the circle and tori, training many runs across multiple dimensions. They find that a standard periodic-feature network often converges to folded almost-everywhere solutions with incorrect values, while some geometry-aware parameterizations recover the correct viscosity solution more reliably. They also propose a mesh-free finite-difference diagnostic based on semiconcavity that can detect these bad solutions without access to the exact answer.
pairs.new:
Shows PINNs can drive the residual to zero while converging to an O(1)-wrong Hamilton-Jacobi solution.
Studies a fixed-horizon pursuit-evasion game on S1, T2, and T4 where the Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs value is known exactly, training four neural parameterizations with ten seeds each for 120 runs. A standard Fourier-feature network found folded almost-everywhere solutions in all 30 runs; a periodic-loss network recovered the viscosity solution in 1D and 2D but not reliably in 4D; geodesic-distance inputs recovered the viscosity solution in all 30 runs for one parameterization and in 27 of 30 for a min-over-charts model, and a semiconcavity-based finite-difference test detected the folded and wrong-image failures without the exact value function.

pairs.title: PINNeval: A Comprehensive Evaluation Standard for Physics-Informed Neural Networks
pairs.abstract: The Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) literature has produced a rapidly expanding catalogue of methods. We divide a PINN training pipeline systematically into four components and observe that many existing benchmarks study these components in isolation. These components are domain-importance adaptation, loss balancing, neural network architecture, and optimization scheme. Moreover, the studies set the surrounding and not considered components of the pipeline to a minimal default that is no longer representative of current best practice approaches. Conclusions drawn under such conditions may not transfer to competitive pipelines. In this work, we propose a new evaluation protocol that (1) treats the four components as an integrated system; (2) crucially requires competitive implementations of the components not under investigation; (3) specifies the metrics and reporting format; and (4) is accompanied by structured documentation that ensures the traceability of evaluations across studies. Based on this comprehensive protocol, we release PINNpipe, an innovative JAX package containing 18 different methods from the current literature as well as nine efficiently implemented benchmark problems. Using PINNpipe, we illustrate our evaluation protocol in relation to established benchmark studies and report results that challenge common assumptions.
pairs.old: The paper addresses evaluation practices for physics-informed neural networks by proposing a standardized protocol for comparing methods across the full training pipeline. It breaks the pipeline into four interacting components—domain-importance adaptation, loss balancing, network architecture, and optimization—and argues that prior benchmarks often isolate one component while leaving the others at outdated defaults. To support the protocol, the authors release PINNpipe, a JAX package with 18 methods and nine benchmark problems. Using this framework, they show that results from conventional benchmark setups can differ substantially from those obtained under more competitive implementations.
pairs.new:
Introduces PINNeval, a protocol that evaluates PINNs as an integrated pipeline with competitive defaults for untargeted components.
The paper splits PINN training into four components—domain-importance adaptation, loss balancing, neural network architecture, and optimization scheme—and argues that many benchmarks isolate one while leaving the others at minimal defaults. It proposes an evaluation protocol that treats all four as a system, requires competitive implementations for components not under study, fixes metrics and reporting, and is paired with PINNpipe, a JAX package with 18 methods and 9 benchmark problems; the authors use it to reproduce established benchmark settings and report results that challenge common assumptions.
